On section 273-filing and publication of joint tariffs,

This section seems to introduce a new principle into the Act, that is, not allowing a company to charge lower rates than the rates approved of by the board. I think the companies ought to be allowed to charge lower rates provided they do not discriminate against individuals or places. If the company think it is to their interest, perhaps at a particular season of the year, when they are competing with water transportation, to charge lower rates than those fixed by the board, why should they not be allowed to do so ?

i.M) CANALS. In cases in which it is necessary that the company shall act promptly, that is to say, in all cases where the rates require to be fixed for competitive purposes, that is allowed. But where there is ample time, it has been deemed proper and reasonable that the company should prepare their tariff, notify the board, and give them a copy of the tariff. The board is thus put in possession of the intentions of the company. It is to enable the board to keep close supervision over, the railways, and to have always before them knowledge of what is going on, that this provision is made. There is ample opportunity in ordinary transactions for them to do this. In extraordinary and emergency cases there is not, and therefore we have made it permissible for the railway companies, under what they call the competitive tariff, to make their tariff on the instant; and all they have to do is to forward that tariff at once, so that it may be known to the board that such a tariff on a competitive basis has been made.

Suppose a case like this occurs. Freight is being carried from the port of Buffalo on the American side to Montreal. The Canadian Pacific Railway has a line between these two points, on which the rate is fixed by the commission. Some time or other they may have to compete with the American route for the traffic. Is there any provision in the Bill which would allow them to do that ?
It would be allowed on competitive business.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
Suppose the railway were competing with water transportation, it would be allowed to lower its rates. But fifty or sixty times in the year a foreign railway company, when they find that the rate's on our railways are fixed
between Buffalo and Montreal and that they could not charge any less without the consent of the board, might immediately lower their rates and take the whole of the freight from our railways. It seems to me that more elasticity should be allowed to the companies.	*

1 think that the hon. member for Lanark (Hon. Mr. Haggart) is perfectly right. In the United States that principle has been adopted. I notice that in one instance from Kansas city to Buffalo, while fixed rates were something like 12 cents, the actual rate charged was 5 cents per one hundred pounds. The same thing applied between Chicago and Buffalo. When the water rates come in, if you tied the railways up to a certain rate, they could not do anything at all. So long as they do not discriminate, I think you should allow them to cut rates as low as possible.

The difficulty I see about the principle which the hon. minister is trying to establish is this, that it virtually makes the board traffic manager of all the railways. They have to know everything that goes on from week to week, settle the rates, variable as those must be according to the exigencies of business. The hon. gentleman says that an emergency caii be met by the company acting upon it and afterwards giving reasonable explanation, but apart from emergency altogether, the traffic manager of a railway has from time to time to consider all the surroundings, and while lie cannot raise the tariff rates he may be forced, by circumstances beyond his control to carry for less than those rates. If the board must be consulted on all these occasions, they will be virtually traffic managers of the road and be given all the discretion that ought to be given the officials of a road carrying on a commercial business. The hon. gentleman has not shown ns the necessity for this. He has told us what he intends doing and why he thinks there is no difficulty, but how this will benefit the public he has not said, and I should think that there ought to be some very good reason indeed why a railway should not be allowed to charge as little as it likes, provided it charges everybody on the same scale.

The hon. gentleman must see the importance, the absolute necessity of the board being advised of changes in rates, if it is to exercise proper supervision over these rates. No one imagines that any railway commission would lie averse to a railway company carrying its traffic at the lowest possible rate, and there will be no fault found with any tariff which a railway company may propose because the rates are too low unless it be a discriminatory tariff. But unless you have some sort of control over
56S3

tlie tariff which they make, how are you to juuge whether or not the company are discriminating ? The hoard will then he at a great loss to form a judgment and to deal with the question of discrimination in an efficient manner. If you are to allow a railway company, without the knowledge of the railway commission, to reduce tins rates, you will be undermining one of the safeguards provided in this Bill for the public protection. I have listened carefully to the objection made on behalf of the railways, but I do not see that I could abolish this principle in the Bill without greatly weakening and impairing the control of rates by the board. With these tariffs before it, the board will be able to see whether or not: rates are being lowered in one direction or another for the purpose of discrimination, One ol' the things that the people most complain of is discrimination, and wherever it exists it ought to be stopped, and we are moving in that direction.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I would like the hon. gentleman to consider whether he is not, by the method he is adopting, destroying in fact the competition between railway companies. I suppose he will concede that in a particular district, when the board settles the tariff, it will settle it for all railway companies. That being so, the board says to each railway company : Ton must carry at such a rate and no lower, but it is not uncommon that all the, railway companies in tlie same district will not have exactly the same opinion as to how low a rate they can charge. Take the Canadian Pacilic Railway and the Grand Trunk Railway, the Grand Trunk Railway may be of opinion that it could carry at a live cent rate and the Canadian Pacific Railway might be of the opinion that it would require a six cent rate. The board, by its decision, might deprive the public of the benefit of the lower late.

Where competition exists, each company may make its rates. There is nothing in this Act which suggests that a railway company may not charge lower rates than the tariff. On the contrary, the probability is recognized that that will be done. A railway company may make its rate as low as it pleases. All it has to do is to file its tariff and the board will not disallow it except where it is a discriminating tariff.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: How would the hon. gentleman deal with the ease where one railway wanted to carry at the rate of five cents and the other wanted to charge six cents.

The hon. gentleman is talking about one railway now against another. But the question of discrimination does not arise in such a case. The question of discrimination. Mr. BLAIR.
tion arises when a railway company deals differently with its own customers.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I am speaking about tariffs which have been approved by the board. The tariff is binding on both companies. If one is willing to carry for less than that and the other is not, and you prevent one fr. m carrying at a less rate than that fixed by the tariff, you prevent competition.

Not at all. I must have failed altogether to make my meaning clear. I defy my hon. friend to point to a single syllable that will prevent competition. On the contrary everything points to competition. We do not require a tariff to be filed before a competitive rate is made.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I am not talking about an emergency tariff.

Neither am I. The question is as to competition. Whenever a railway is offered competitive business, business which another railway could get, if they do not take it, they are authorized to make a rate of what they please and take the business. The only thing is that they must give the board notice by filing the memoran dum showing the tariff they made on the business. Then they justify the tariff by the fact that they are giving it to get the business. Is that calculated to discourage competition ? I think not.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
The hon. minister's explanation seems so entirely different from the section itself. The section is :
And upon any such joint tariff being so duly filed and published, and published as provided in section 274, the company or companies shall, unless such tariff is disallowed by the board, charge the toll or tolls as specified therein, but until such tariff is so duly filed and published. no such toll or tolls shall be charged by the company or companies.

The hon. gentleman is not dealing with the question. The clause the hon. gentleman has read is not the only clause of the Bill bearing upon the general question of tariff. 'This is a clause relating to joint tariffs upon a continuous through-route business-where one railway hauls a part of the way and another must haul the rest, and they have a joint tariff. There are a great many branches and subdivisions of the tariff question, and it is very important not to confuse them, because it is impossible to discuss them intelligently if you do.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Though this applies to joint tariffs, still fhe principle is there. A competitive tariff can be arranged where two roads must take part in the haul just the same as where the haul is altogether by one road.
Certainly.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The same principle applies to the joint tariff as to the other. My opinion is that under this clause the company should be allowed to charge anything under the amount of toll approved of by the board, without furnishing the department of the government with the information, provided they do not discriminate in a joint tariff against any individual or place.

How would it be possible to insure the possession by the board of such information as would enable them to determine whether there was discrimination or not, if you allow the companies to make such charge as they please without furnishing the information as to what charge they have made ?
Hon. Mr. HAGGART What possible object is it for the board to know. They only want to know whether there has been discrimination or not. But, if there has been no discrimination against an individual or against a place, what possible object is it for the board to know whether the tariff charged is lower than that allowed by the board or not ?
speakername: The MINISTER OP RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The hon. gentleman starts out with the assumption-a very extraordinary thing for him to do-that there is no discrimination. I am trying to point out to him that somebody must determine whether there is discrimination or not and lie cannot determine that unless the rates are made known.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: And would the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Blair) be kind enough to tell me how the board could know from merely seeing the rate whether there was discrimination or not ?
When they have the facts
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The question of discrimination will only come up if there is a complaint raised. The person making the complaint would know whom to accuse of receiving the advantage, and that person could be brought before the board and made to give evidence as to the rate. The fact is that the hon. minister, to facilitate the trying of cases before the board, is destroying competition.	[DOT]
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Barker) is altogether mistaken.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
The hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker) has said that the effect of this was to destroy competition. It seems to me that is the pith of the whole argument. I would like to give a concrete illustration of something that came under my notice a year or two ago. It relates to the matter of fuel oil. When the Standard Oil Company came into Canada, they
raised the price of fuel oil to nearly double what it was before.
In what year ?

About two or three years ago. The Canadian railways, the Grand Trunk and the Canadian Pacific Railway, saw that by water competition they would be deprived of carrying a certain amount of refined oil such as they had carried previous to the time the Standard Oil Company came into Canada. The rates from the fields where the oil was produced were, for refined oil 15 cents per 100 pounds, and for fuel oil, which is a by-product of the other, 9 cents per 100 pounds. The two Canadian railways abandoned the rate of 9 cents on fuel oil, "which was worth about $1.50 a barrel against about $7 for refined oil, and allowed the fuel oil to come under the rate of freight on refined oil. So far as Toronto and every other town in Ontario east of Toronto was concerned, this rate held. But the Michigan Central has connection into Hamilton, and it refused to adopt the ruling of the other railways but went on carrying oil at 9 cents per 100 pounds as it had been carried for many years before. Now, under the provision proposed by the hon. minister with regard to this matter, that kind of competition will be destroyed.
I do not think it at all.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: If the railway cannot make traffic at a lower rate of freight than those filed with the government, it seems to me that destroys competition.

We have passed a number of clauses dealing with the general subject of rates. We have passed clauses relating to the subject of reducing rates without a word of criticism, nor -would criticism have been justified. Read section 262. All this Act requires is that special freight tariffs and competitive tariffs shall be filed with the board, and such tariffs shall state the date when issued, and when to take effect. And the section says :
When any such tariff reduces any toll previously authorized to be charged under this Act

So, reductions are contemplated in plain and explicit terms. The company may reduce its tariff to zero if it will-
-the company shall file such tariff with the board.
And so on. Now, I say that is all, and that tariff, as well as other tariffs, may be disallowed, but disallowed for sufficient cause. It would be disallowed if proved to be a discriminating tariff within the meaning of this Act; if it was not discriminating, no one having any qualifications to be a member of the board would disallow it simply because it reduced the rates. The very point is to get the rates down to a

reasonable and proper basis, and when a railway company reduces, of its own motion, the rates which it charges, surely it is not to be assumed that the railway commission are going to disallow that tariff upon that ground alone. If there is any discrimination about it which will work unjustly to others, then of course the board may properly exercise the discretion with which the law invests them. Now, when we are dealing further along with other phases of the question of charges, of freight and tolls, when we come down to the joint tariff for practically foreign business, all that we provide is that these joint tariffs should be tiled. Now, where is there any possibility of injury to any interest in requiring that these should be filed, and where is the foundation for the suggestion lion, gentlemen have made that we are interfering with competition ? I venture to say it cannot be found in the provisions of this Bill.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The minister will admit that any tariff has to be registered and filed with the commission. Any railroad knowing that its cut rate which is of advantage to the public, was going to be made known to other railroads, would not file. A man would not make the cut rate if lie knew his competitors were going to find it out immediately, and the public would not get the benefit of it.
We are providing that these should not be made public, they are for the private and personal knowledge of the commissioners alone.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: But they are bound to tile every cut rate.

Yes, but they do not publish them, they are simply filed. That it seems to me, is a reasonable and proper precaution; the board should have knowledge of all the rates that are being imposed by the railway companies so that they may, having that knowledge, better decide as to whether or not there is any violation of the law in discriminating against other rights and interests.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I thought that before any special rates took effect they had to be published. First of all, you have to file them with the board and then you have to publish them three days before they take effect.
When any such tariff reduces any toll previously authorized to he charged under this Act, the company shall file such tariff with the board and shall publish the same in the manner in section 274 in such case provided, at least three clear days previous to the date on which such tariff is intended to take effect.
That expressly excludes applications for competitive tariffs. That clause has been amended.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: It seems to me you are abandoning the fundamental principle of the American law, which says that the great and beneficial effect of their board is publicity. You say here that you intend to keep it private.

I would like to be able to satisfy all my hon. friends opposite, but I do not see how I can do so. One says this is going to work unjustly because the competitive tariffs are going to be published; another condemns the Bill because he says that the great merit of the board is publicity.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I am merely drawing attention to that feature of the American law.
I think the hon. member for Toronto (Mr. Kemp) and the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) must harmonize their views if they are going to act as a compact force in hostility to this Bill.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I am sure I am not acting in any hostile way towards this Bill. I think the Bill is a very good one, but I am not clear as to the difference between a competitive tariff and a special tariff. I do not see any place in the Bill where this point is covered. This tariff is not to be published, but the one mentioned in clause 202 is to be made public. Now, where is the clause that refers to special competitive tariffs that are not to be made public.
I suppose subsection 3 of 200 is the one.

You will find it in the amended subsection 4 of section 202. I admit that these are subjects of a technical character [DOT] which the ordinary man is not able to understand without devoting a good deal of attention and study to them. I think that lion, gentlemen opposite, if they desire to assist in putting through the Bill, as I think they do, will have to take for granted that some attention and some study have been given to these things so as to make a scheme workable, without doing any injury to the business of the country. I could hardly be compelled to make hon. gentlemen opposite understand all these provisions when there may be some that I do not clearly understand myself.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: But the trouble with me is that I do not see the difference between a special tariff and a competitive tariff. Would the minister tell me the difference ?

If the hon. gentleman will read the Bill, and is able to understand it, he will see the difference. Differences exist in railway operations and traffic. The law has defined the difference. I presume the

hon. member will not ask me to go over it again and give a rgsumd of the whole definition and description of the whole classes of tariffs.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
No, I will not, particularly as I see that the hon. minister knows nothing about the difference. He has a very clever way of getting around the difficulty.
The MINISTER, OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS. I do not know how the hon. gentleman can say that I do not know anything about it, because he is absolutely without any knowledge himself. I do not know how he will be competent to judge as to the competency of anybody else. This Bill provides for three different classes of freight tariffs. There is the standard freight tariff. That is the maximum. That is the tariff which is prepared by the companies and submitted to the board and if it receives the approval of the board it is the standard tariff that governs. Then, in special cases, in cases of special traffic and special classes of goods, this Bill contemplates that the companies may prepare and submit special freight tariffs. When these special freight tariffs are submitted they may go into operation and the company may make a tariff as low as it pleases as a special freight tariff. It has to be filed and this special freight tariff, if it is not competitive, the Act contemplates, shall be published. There is another class of tariff which is not intended by tlfe company to come within either of these two classes, standard freight or special freight tariff, which may come within the third class which is called the competitive class, and which is designed to encourage competition in the fullest possible degree. That class of tariff may be imposed by the company without the sanction of the board. The company may take shipments under that tariff and the tariff need not be published. It is communicated to the board for the private knowledge and information of the board, and why we require that it should be placed before file board is that the board may have under its hand the means of knowledge so that it can determine whether or not from among the classes of business the company was doing at a certain time it was unduly discriminating in its provisions contrary to the provisions of this Bill. I think it would be difficult to design any more effective means of protecting the public and guarding against improper discrimination and, at the same time affording the freest hand and the widest latitude to railway companies to go on with their business.

Supposing that a railway company which did not make a competitive tariff was suspicious that a railway company which did make one was giving lower rates than authorized by the commission, if it applied to the commission or this competitive tariff, would the commission give it to that railway company ?

That is a matter, which, of course, would necessarily be in the discretion of the commission. If anybody who felt he had a grievance because some lower rate was given by the railway company to his neighbour than to himself came before the railway commission, the commission would say :	Well, what is your complaint,
what is it that you say the company has done for your neighbour ? If the information received from him should be such as to convince the board, or the member of the board that might be going into the matter at the moment, that there was ground to suspect discrimination was going on, it would not be necessary that the board should hand over a copy of this tariff to the complainant. They would be moved to have this thing further inquired into and such definite action taken as they thought proper to take against the company that was discriminating. The design is that this tariff shall not be made public so that opposing railways could know what , a neighbour railway was doing in offering cheap rates. I think it is very proper that such information should be withheld.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
After that explanation I do not see any difference yet between the special freight tariff and the competitive tariff except this; the company has to publish the special freight tariff for a certain number of days and let the public know what it is. The competitive tariff need not be published at all. But, the moment the tariff is approved by the board or filed with the board, the distinction between the competitive and special tariffs ceases.
On subsection (c), section 274-filing and publication of competitive tariffs,

Here is a provision for a competitive tariff, and the distinction between that and the special tariff was that one was to be made public and the other not. Under this section the competitive tariff is obliged to be open for the inspection of the public.
The intention of this is that the board, when they know all the circumstances of the case, may have power to exempt this from publication.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I see that ; but in some cases competitive tariffs are to be published unless the board specially exempts them. It appears to me that a special tariff may be a competitive tariff, and the two things are so closely joined that I cannot see the distinction yet.

I will try to make my hon. friend see the difference between a special tariff

and a competitive tariff. The distinction between these two tariffs does not consist at all in the circumstance that one may be exempted by the board from publication and the other not. A special freight tariff is a tariff which in addition is based upon the rules that govern it and it is controlled by the law on the short haul principle, but the competitive tariff is not.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Might I ask the minister if, under any circumstances, such a thing as a competitive tariff could exist between the city of Ottawa and Peterborough, Ontario, for instance ? There is no water competition.
It would not be limited to water competition.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canada Atlantic Railway and the Grand Trunk Railway go to Peterborough-could a competitive tariff exist between Ottawa and Peterborough ?
There cannot be any possible objection to competition between railroads running between any two points in Canada that are reached by two roads.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Before this section is adopted, I would like to draw the attention of the minister to a matter which I think lie has heard of before. How are the public to know when it is the intention of the committee to revise tariffs or classifications ? I think it was suggested to the minister that notice of all changes of tariff should be sent to certain boards of trade or other com-[DOT] mercial organizations. It has been the complaint of these organizations for a long time past that they have not known of these changes, and have not been able to present the. case of the public. Is there any way that the minister can suggest whereby notice of these changes could be made known to these organizations ?
Certain boards of trade might be notified.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
Something like the following has been suggested :
The company shall file with the board as many copies of all proposed tariffs and freight classifications as the hoard may prescribe, and on receipt thereof the secretary of the board shall mail to each incorporated board of trade, chamber of commerce or commercial association in Canada a copy thereof, and shall send by mail a copy thereof to all other persons requiring the same.
I think fifty or sixty copies would be sufficient.

I think we might make provision very easily ; but I would not advise as many copies as'that. There are only three Hon. Mr. BLAIR.
or four boards of trade that interest themselves in the subject. The Toronto Board of Trade is the only one with which I have had any communication on the subject.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: It represents pretty well the Ontario organizations.
I think I would not be far astray if I said that one of our great railroads would have a thousand different tariffs in operation, and it would be a very serious matter to give notice of all these.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The hoards of trade look upon it as a very important matter.

That is true, and I think the case would be met sufficiently by providing that the boards of trade of Toronto and Montreal should be supplied. Tjiey are the great centres, and perhaps would be the only ones requiring to be informed.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: You might provide for sending to cities of over 200,000 population.
I will look into the matter, and put something in the Bill.	[DOT]
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
If the minister adopts that clause or any modification of it, I would suggest that he would provide for sending to all cities where there are boards of trade.
On section 279, subsection 3,
3. Any person or any officer or ageht of any company who shall deliver goods for transportation to the company or for whom as consignor or consignee the company shall transport goods, who shall knowingly or wilfully, by false billing, false classification, false weighing, false representation of the contents of the package, or false report of weight, or by any other device or means, whether with or without the consent or connivance of the company, its agent or agents, obtain transportation for such goods at less than the regular tolls then authorized and in force on the railway shall for each offence be liable to a penalty of not exceeding one thousand dollars nor less than ore hundred dollars.

I do not understand what the object is of making a double penalty for the shipper. The railway company, under the two preceding sections are liable to a flue of from $100 to $1,000. Under subsection 3, the shipper is liable to a similar penalty. But why put into the hands of the railway power practically to fine the shipper and hold his goods and confiscate them to pay the fine ?

The object is to provide all necessary and proper, and possible guarantees that the law shall be enforced. In replying to what I understand to be the hon. member's (Mr. Kemp) view, I do not see why one of the parties should be subject to a penalty and the other, who may have wilfully incited or encouraged

the unlawful act, should escape. We make both liable and put both on the same basis.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I think the hon. minister does not understand me. I agree that the shipper should be subject to the penalties which are prescribed in subsection 3, which are the same as those prescribed against the railway. But the hon. minister not only subjects the shipper, to the same fines as the railway company-to which I agree- but he allows the railway company to charge fifty per cent more if freight is not classified in the way prescribed.
It is the fifty per cent tariff the hon. gentleman objects to ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I object to the double fine against the shipper. I may refresh the hon. minister's memory by again calling his attention to something I spoke of in the House a few days ago. The railway companies issued a classification which was to take effect on the 1st of May. Under the law, that should be submitted to the Governor in Council and approved. This has not been done, but yet the railways are operating under it. It may be said that the classification is not more onerous to the shipper than the schedule of a previous time. I am not speaking of the classification itself, but of a rule inserted in the front of this classification. To this rule I drew attention before. It provides that if articles are shipped under false names to deceive the carrier or avoid the classification, the agent is to charge fifty per cent in addition to the rate that would have been charged had the property been correctly described. So, the hon. minister will see that the railways, while they occupy the same position as the shipper with regard to the penalty of from $100 to $1,000, they have asked-I take it-the hon. minister to empower them by legislation to inflict a double penalty upon the shipper. I take it that the attention of the hon. minister has not been drawn to the fact that the shipper is already subjected to the same penalty as the railways, and should not be subjected to the double penalty at the hands of the railways without coming before the commission.

If I understand what the hon. gentleman (Mr. Kemp) has in mind, I must say that I cannot agree with him. The1 penalties imposed under this clause are not because the shipper is trying to cheat the railways, but for the purpose of securing the observance of the law. When the fine is imposed, it does not go into the exchequer of the railway. In the other case where the extra rate of fifty jier cent in addition to the ordinary rate is allowed, that is for the protection of the railways. Suppose that a railway carries a cargo of grain the freight on which would be, for the
sake of illustration, $200, but stowed away in that grain are ten or fifteen thousand dollars worth of very high class, rich goods, which, if properly billed would pay very high rates, the hauling of these goods being very profitable to the railway. If a man is trying to have carried as grain, goods that should be charged four to twenty times as high it is reasonable not only that he should pay a penalty for his fault, but that he should pay a higher rate to the railway company than he would be called upon to pay under ordinary circumstances. It is not a very excessive penalty that is imposed in this way. He only pays one-half more freight than he would have paid if the railway company were carrying the article under its proper classification. There seems to be no reason why, when fraud is being practiced upon the company, and they discover it, the shipper should not pay additional freight. That, at all events, is the reason why this clause has been inserted. I have talked the matter over fully with the railway people, and they made cut a case that satisfied me this was a fair proposition.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: It seems to me there is not sufficient reason to make the distinction between the punishment provided in subsection 3 and the punishment provided in the other sections. The shipper who commits the fraud described in subsection 3 incurs a punishment similar to the punishment provided in the other subsections. He is liable to pay a sum of from $100 to $1,000, and he is punished for that offence. Why should he be punished twice ? There is no doubt that under the common law, if that fraud is discovered and he is convicted, the railway company has a claim against him for the full amount ; and if, as mentioned by the Minister of Railways, he has stored that grain or other articles, he might be subject to the full amount of his freight, I think the Minister of Railways will admit that, without the proposed amendment. The fraud has been discovered. We will suppose he has paid his fine, and he is subject to the full amount of his freight under the common law. Then why should we subject him to this 50 per cent additional ? I say that he has purged his fault by the payment of his fine. It seems to me that the railway companies are demanding a little too much when, after he has paid his fine, they wish him in addition to pay 50 per cent more. He becomes, under these circumstances^ liable to a double penalty. I think it would be better to leave it as it is.

I do not know that I can add anything to what I have said. It still seems to me reasonable that a man who has been caught in the act of practising a fraud in getting his goods carried at a rate much below the proper rate, should, when discovered, be called upon to pay something in addition

to the price of that freight, because that is the only mode in which the company can protect itself. The railway company may perhaps, in the course of the year's business, carry a good deal of freight under those circumstances and in that way, without discovering the fraud, and after sustaining a loss. But when a man is caught operating in such a fashion, I do not think we are treating him unjustly when we say that, in addition to the proper rate of freight which he would have to pay, he should pay an additional sum to the company whom he may have defrauded in many instances. So far as the penalty is concerned, that is a separate proposition. But I do not see why we should feel any concern at all as respects the individual who is caught perpetrating such acts. He does not deserve any sympathy.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
This is another illustration of the plausible way the railways have of putting their case before the minister. I would like to ask the minister if the railways can cite a case where grain was ever carried in car-loads as silverware, or other expensive material ? I do not deny but that it might be done. A man who would do that would steal, he would do anything; and there ought to be a law to reach such individuals. But under the Act, as the minister had it originally drawn, that man is subject to a penalty of .$1,000 if he is discovered. Now, that is an extreme case, and it is another indication of the plausible and clever way the railways have of working. I venture to say that such a case never happened. But I wish to refer to the thousands and thousands of shipments that take place every day, from every warehouse in the country and from every factory in the country, which would be affected by this clause. Now, in that classification there are upwards of 3.000 different items. That classification is not carefully studied by the clerk in the employ of the manufacturer or the merchant : it is a most complicated document, and it is possible for a clerk to make a mistake. If he makes a wilful mistake, he can be punished. But this clause goes further, and as soon as the goods which are shipped reach the railway station they are subject to an inspection-by whom ? They are subject to the inspection of men appointed by the railways. These men sometimes know their business, but very frequently they know very little about what the goods are that are shipped. After making their inspection, they raise the billing of these goods, and they walk into the office of the billing clerk of the railway company and they say : Inflict a penalty on this man of 50 per cent over and above the freight of these goods, because they are wrongly billed. Who is to try the case ? The man is not asked. The railway people never go to the shipper and ask him why he did this, and get an explanation. Still they are just Hon. Mr. BLAIR.
as liable to be in the wrong as the shipper. They are more frequently in error than the shipper, in my experience, and I have had a good deal of experience with them. And to say that a man should be subject to a. penalty of $1,000 for committing such a mistake, and that his goods are liable to be confiscated by the railway with 50 per cent addition-I say it is an outrage, and the public of this country will consider it as such if it is persisted in. I would like to know where there is a precedent in Great Britain or the United States for such action. I say the dishonest shipper that will wrongfully classify his goods should be brought under the Criminal Code. I do not complain that he should be fined $1,000. even $2,000. Put him in jail if necessary ; but do not leave it in the hands of the railway to administer the criminal laws of this country.

It is not proposed that the railways shall administer the criminal law. They cannot even enforce any of these penalties under this Act without leave of the board. But this is a case where a man has wilfully committed a fraud. He is not, as the hon. gentleman has just pictured him, an innocent man who has made a mistake by reason of the great extent and variety of the classification which he has not been able to understand. This is the case of a man who wilfully perpetrates or attempts to perpetrate a fraud upon the company in the transportation of his goods. WThy should not that man be asked to pay more than the ordinary rate that he has tried to escape by getting freight carried for less ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Who is to say whether he did it wilfully or knowingly ?
The court.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I do not understand that the court would have to say it at all. The railway company would hold the man's goods, if the fraud is made plain under this classification. I am advised that the railway company could collect the fine as an extra charge and hold the man's goods until he paid it.

The question is raised as to whether a man has done it wilfully and knowingly. The railway company cannot determine whether it has been done wilfully or knowingly, but if it were done wilfully and knowingly they would have the right, under this Bill, to insist upon the payment of the fine.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I think justice will be accomplished if the merchant were compelled to pay his proper rate without imposing a penalty of fifty per cent, because he is made to pay the company a penalty in addition of from $100 to $1,000.
He may or lie may not. He is subject to it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: This subsection contemplates that the railway company may commit an offence against the merchant. In that case the railway company has to pay a fine, but it has not to pay the merchant anything. If the merchant commits an offence he has not only to pay a fine, but he has to pay something to the railway company. I do not know that the penalty will do any good to the railway company. The punishment of this fine will deter the merchant from improperly representing his freight, and I think it will answer all the purposes if the hon. minister simply requires the merchant to pay the full rate he should have paid in addition to the fine. I think my hon. friend from East Toronto (Mr. Kemp) is quite right in saying that you are dealing differently with the merchant from the way in which you are dealing with the railway company.

I would like to ask the hon. minister how this penalty of 50 per cent in addition is to be collected ? It is an extra toll. The railway will hold that freight until it is paid. Does the hon. minister pretend to say that the freight in each case of the hundreds of thousands of cases that will occur will be held until this matter is brought to the attention of the commission sitting in Ottawa, or some place else, before it is decided ? You would take up all the time of the commission if that procedure had to be gone to. The 50 per cent extra is in the shape of a toll and it would be collected by the railways, and if the consignee refuses to pay it, the railways will have the same power they have now in reference to any toll, to realize upon the goods.

I will consider this subsection, and in the meantime we will allow it to stand if hon. gentlemen think it is unduly favourable to the railway company.
On subsection 5, section 279,
Whenever the company files with the board and publishes any tariff, and such tariff comes into force and is not disallowed by the board, under this Act, or participates in any such tariff, the tolls in such tariff, while so in force, shall as against such company, its officers, agents or employees, in any prosecution under this Act, be conclusively deemed to be the legal tolls chargeable by such company, and any departure therefrom shall be an offence under this Act.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Does that mean that they may file a lower or higher tariff than that which has been approved by the board ?
This applies to any tariff. Of course, the company could not have any tariff higher than the standard tariff.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I think the word ' disallowed ' is very dangerous. The theory of the Bill is that we are changing altogether the old system by which the railway company originated a tariff, put it in force, and the Railway Committee of the Privy Council would disallow it. Now a tariff is to be in effect only after it is allowed by the railway commission. It is quite true the company may originate it in the way of proposing it, but it gets its force and effect from the action of the board and from that alone. It has no force or effect until the board sactions it, and it is on that point that a difficulty may arise.
There are certain tariffs which may be filed and which do not require to be allowed or disallowed.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: If the railway company conceives that a certain tariff ought not be submitted to the board, and they do not comply with these terms they are subject to all the penalties herein laid down. I think it is giving the railways a large and dangerous amount of control.
It is the railways that are subject to these penalties.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: That does not alter the case, because I suppose the railway company has the same right as anybody else. I am not fighting for farmers or merchants or any particular class. I am calling the attention of the minister to the effect of this on the people, no matter who these people happen to be.
It is not for but against the railway company.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
It is giving the railway company in the meantime an enormous control.
On subsection 6,

I move to add to subsection 6 the following
Provided that upon the hearing and determination of any application or complaint before the board in respect of any such infraction, the board may in addition to or in substitution of any other relief, award to any complaining parties so aggrieved such damages as it may find him to have sustained, and the payment of such award shall be in complete satisfaction of any claim for damages, including repayment of over charges which such party would otherwise have had by reason of such infraction or matters of complaint.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: What is the meaning of this ?

This was in the Bill introduced last year, but on consideration we thought we had better drop it. However, this



clause is in the English Act and is worked by the English Board of Railway Commissioners, and we are led to believe that it has answered a very useful purpose. The railwav board having all the evidence before it, it would seem that they might very properly consider the question and make the award of damages to the person who suffered, and if dealt with in that way that is the end of the litigation. This law prevails in England and it has a good deal-to recommend it. It is not of course entirely free from doubt, but it would be a very easy matter if it is found not to achieve any good purpose, to eliminate it from the Bill at any time. We have the English experience for a number of years to justify us in trying the experiment.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Has it been construed in England as ousting the jurisdiction of the courts with respect to damages.
I think so.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
Either this subsection 6 as originally printed should be allowed to stand without this addition, or if this addition be inserted then we had better remove the most of subsection 6. I submit that subsection 6 without this addition is quite plain enough in giving the right of action in an ordinary court of justice. It is not a question for the jurisdiction of the board at all. If it is fair that a company should be liable to make good in treble damages the amount of loss sustained, then this further provision should not be inserted to conflict with it.
In the first place, if the party aggrieved does not contemplate getting his whole remedy before the board, but contemplates bringing an action at law at a later date, he will not bring before the board evidence to show the full relief he is entitled to. Many cases will arise in the working out of this Act in which evidence will come before the board to put the board to some extent in possession of the facts. But where a suitor or party complaining does not intend to submit his rights to the board for determination of the damage lie shall sustain, I submit that it would be unfair to deprive him of the ordinary rights which are directly conferred upon him undef subsection 6 unless with his consent. If lie sees fit to consent to it, I do not see any great difficulty ; but I submit that if there is any such proviso put in, although I am [DOT]not in favour of it being put in at all, it should read that the board may, ' with the eonsent of the party complaining, but not otherwise,' do so and so. It is a case in which we are giving to the board controlling powers which I do not think are required in order to the efficient carrying out of the provisions of this Act.
I am willing to insert the words,
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: ' with the consent of the parties.' I do not think the board would act without their consent.

I am inclined to think that there must be some change made in the section, otherwise it would not work out very well. For example, suppose that a person who believes himself to be aggrieved has begun an action against a company in the courts. Under the section as printed, he would be entitled to recover from the railway company. While that action was pending, a similar application might be made to the board under the provisions of this statute; and unless this section were amended in some way, yon would have the court and the board both dealing with the same matter at the same time. It seems to me that some confusion would be likely to ensue unless you had some language to show where the jurisdiction of the board ceased and the jurisdiction of the court began.
THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS. It would seem to me that even though the proceedings had been commenced, the adjudication would be made by the board.

Curiously enough I had almost the very case I refer to. The hon. gentleman may remember that there used to be a board of arbitrators in connection with the government railway. An action was commenced by an individual whose land was taken, against the .officers of the government on the ground that the statute was not complied with before the land was entered upon. A line exceeding one mile in length on the Dartmouth branch had been commenced without an Order in Council being issued, though it could only be done by virtue of an Order in Council. While that action was pending, the O'-der in Council was passed, and proceedings were taken before the arbitrators, and the damages, being the value of the land, were assessed. Then the question arose whether or not that could be pleaded as a good matter arising after the action commenced. Tlir court held that it could not. Perhaps it would be advisable to be pretty definite in regard to these two branches of the section otherwise you might have considerable litigation as to whether or not the application had been answered.
Subsection 6 allowed to stand.
On section 284-traffic agreements.

I move that this section be amended by adding at the end of subsection 1 the following words :
Provided that the board may by order or regulation, exempt the company from complying with any of the foregoing conditions with respect to any such agreement or arrangement made or entered into by the company for the transaction of the usual and ordinary business
[DOT]5701

of the company, and where such consent of the shareholders may be deemed by the board to be unnecessary.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: This seems to be a very sweeping exception.

What is intended to be covered is any ordinary traffic agreement which may be made between two tariff officers, and which it is not necessary to have formally ratified by the shareholders. To go through all this formality with regard to a mere arrangement for an interchange of freight would be unnecessary.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: But might not this refer to agreements entered into for a term of years, for example. I should think it would be very dangerous to allow agreements to be entered into for a term of years without the consent of the shareholders.
But agreements may be entered into for a week or a month-a mere part of the ordinary business. The board is empowered to dispense with the formalities in that case.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: But this clause has been in the Railway Act for twenty years and has never interfered with the ordinary interchange of traffic between companies.

They have simply disregarded it.
Section, as amended, agreed to.

speakeroldname: Mr. A. T. THOMPSON (Haldimand and Monck).
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker. Before this motion is passed, I desire to make a few remarks concerning the present condition of the Canadian militia, its wants and the best way of meeting them. I have not spoken this session on this subject, nor will I now treat of it at great length. Fully aware as I am of the difficulty of getting the ear of this House at any time, and more especially at this late season of the session, I bespeak the attention of the honourable members, for I feel that I have matter of importance to lay before them. When his main estimates were under discussion, the Minister of Militia stated that later on, when he brought down the supplementaries, he would make a full statement as to militia affairs in general. I am purposely anticipating this because I wish to give him an opportunity of hearing in advance what I have to say, so that if he sees fit he may later comment upon it, having had plenty of time to verify my facts and figures iii the meantime. I am sorry indeed that he is not present, but I can delay my remarks no longer, since I am momentarily expecting a telegram which may call me away from Ottawa for a indefinite time ; what I say, however, will appear in Hansard, and so be available to him. I may remark that while I do not claim to have a mandate from the militiamen of Canada, I have talked with scores of them since our camps of last fall, have studied the subject as carefully as possible, and am prepared to give an earnest opinion even though a few may be found to differ with it. I am encouraged to proceed in this matter by the feeling that only a few members of this House are absolutely indifferent to our militia, while the number of those actually antagonistic to it is insignificant indeed. We have had encouraging and sympathetic speeches from the member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) who most certainly will not be accused of a-tendency towards militarism, from the member, the independent member, for West Elgin (Mr. Robinson) who will certainly not be accused of extravagance, from the members of His Majesty's truely styled ' Loyal Opposition,' and from a number of others on your right, Sir. But encouraging as all this undoubtedly is, it is as nothing compared with my feeling of satisfaction when I read the memo, of August 11, 1902, presented by our ministers in London to the British ministers there on the subject of imperial defence at the time of the colonial conference last summer. I would very

gladly read that admirable document in toto, Sir, but for fear of wearying the patience of the House, none too robust in weather such as this, and I feel constrained to quote portions of it since upon it in very large measure, I rest my case. First, then, in regretfully declining to meet the suggestions of Mr. St. John Broderick, suggestions which in my opinion, apart altogether from questions of self-government, involved a much heavier expense than that hon. gentleman, unacquainted apparently with our wage market here, had imagined, an expense for which the people of Canada might not have been willing to stand, our ministers state that their objections arise 'not so much from the expense involved,' &c. I note this implied expression of willingness to spend a reasonable sum, for future use in this speech, and proceed with my extracts from the memo :
They fully appreciate the duty of the Dominion, as it advances in population and wealth to make more liberal outlay for those necessary preparations of self defence which every country has to assume and bear.
Further on, in saying a good word for our force, attention is called with pride to * the fact that:
Annual drill in camps of instruction for the rural corps, and at Battalion Headquarters for the city corps, has been carried out each year for the past six years.
Proceeding the ministers say that they are far from claiming that perfection has been attained:
If defects exist

Say they :
-there is every desire on the part of the Canadian government to remove them, and for this purpose the advice and assistance of experienced imperial officers will be welcomed and all reasonable efforts made to secure an efficient system.
Apart from this special memo., on page 32 of the report, we read an account of the discussion of the proposal of Mr. St. John Broderick for a colonial reserve; * a special body of troops, earmarked for imperial service',' the part of which germane to my remarks runs as follows :
The representatives of Canada and Australia were of opinion that the best course to pursue was to endeavour to raise the standard of training for the general body of their forces, to organize the departmental services, and equipment required for the mobilization of a field force, leaving it to the colony, when the need arose to determine how-, and to what extent it should render assistance.
Taking all these quotations together, we find an absolute pledge given by our representatives for militia betterment, a pledge given on an occasion of grave importance, reduced to writing, mistake or misunderstanding an impossibility. Let me recall for a moment the personnel of our representatives on that occasion. There was the Mr. THOMPSON CHaldimand).
Right Hon. Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), wTho has honoured our force by becoming the honorary lieutenant colonel of that smart French Canadian corps, the 9th Yoltigeurs de Quebec ; there wTas the hon. Minister of Finance (Hon. Mr. Fielding) who so constantly and carefully guards the treasury from leakage, there was the hon. Minister of Customs (Hon. Mr. Paterson), not a warlike man, it is true, but an eminently good business one, little likely to be carried away by the showy, side of imperialism, whose department in large part furnishes the funds, a part of which I crave for our necessities ; there was the hon. Minister of Militia (Hon. Sir Frederick Borden) whose knowledge of and warm interest in the force which he directs is too well known to require commendation at my hands, and there was that shrewd and economical administrator the hon. Postmaster General (Hon. Sir William Mulock). Of him let me say a special word. Again and again have I heard him described as unfriendly to the militia. A more unfair charge was never put upon a public man. True, he has spoken out both manfully and well against militarism, but militarism implies a large standing force with a heavy expenditure, it is the very antithesis of a citizen soldiery, and as unpopular with our men to-day as with any other class in the community. His views, embodied in the memo, from which I have quoted give the lie to his slanderers, and enable us to claim him as one of our most valued friends.
Now, Sir, to come from generalities to particulars, from the foundation to the superstructure. While not one of those imperial officers from across the sea whose advice and assistance is to be welcomed as stated in one of the numerous quotations above given, the door is surely wide open also for the advice and assistance of ' one of the native born.' Am I not justified then in supposing that if I can convince this House that the Canadian army is in serious danger of disintegration in one of its very most important parts, relief will be granted, even though that may entail expense ? Am 1 not justified still further in the assumption that once let the cabinet be convinced that the militia is not even stationary but actually retrogressing, this cabinet pledged to Britain for improvement, and it must and will gladly meet the situation and destroy the danger ?
Well Sir, in all seriousness, after due consideration and recognizing the importance of the assertion, I say here to-day in my place in parliament that the militia, so far as the rural part thereof is concerned, is in infinitely worse plight to-day than it was two years ago, and that in my opinion another year under present conditions will utterly demoralize it.
The reason is not far to seek-it lies in the fifty cent daily wage. The time has come, Sir, to double that amount. For many

years the militia struggled on for half a dollar a day, never satisfactorily progressing, ever calling for sacrifice on the part of officers and men. With the increased prosperity of the country, and the higher wages obtainable, the system has broken down. I do not blame this government and its predecessor for getting a fairly good article as cheaply as possible, but since we still require the fairly good article, and can no longer get it at the bargain counter, we must pay whatever higher price is necessary to procure it.
X shall not Sir, make mere empty statements, but I shall substantiate them by facts and figures. Let us see what happened at the recent camps in districts one and two, held respectively at London and at Niagara-on-the-Lake, I think I may say without fear of contradiction two of the best militia districts we have in Canada, but first, for the benefit of the large number of members not acquainted with the technical details, just a word as to the basis on which our force is established. Let me take a company of infantry for example. Our authorized strength for such is three officers, six non-commissioned officers, and thirty-six men. This is on. a peace footing. On a war footing the number of officers and non-commissioned officers would remain precisely the same, but the number of men would be increased to 119, bringing a company exclusive of officers up to a strength of 125, thus making an eight company regiment, 1,000 strong.
Of course the idea was to give us the requisite number of trained officers and noncommissioned officers, with a fair sprinkling of drilled men in the ranks, hoping and believing that under such circumstances the infusion of new blood could be readily absorbed and controlled. This is known as the skeleton system, and considering our resources in men and money would answer very well if adhered to every year. Unfortunately this is not being done. Last year only the non-commissioned officers with one officer per company, and a small number of men. the latter for fatigue work only, and not for drill, were called out. This year all officers and non-commissioned officers, with twenty-one men per company, as against an establishment of thirty-six men, have been called out in the case of most regiments, though some have been left at home entirely. Well Sir, this means that starting as a sekeleton we have been called upon to parade as the skeleton of a skeleton. But worse is yet to follow. The number this year called out would mean about 253 for an eight company infantry regiment, while the figures which I shall presently submit prove that we have been unable to supply even this small quota, not a single regiment that I know of having turned out a full ISO out of the 253 required with the exception of the 30th Wellington rifles, which is a ten company corps. I have shown that
we were called upon to furnish the skeleton of a skeleton, I now state that we have actually turned out the shadow of a skeleton of a skeleton. Can anything so ghost-like be longer called a militia force. True the officers and non-commissioned officers, the most important part, showed up in very fair numbers, but this will not continue. Men must have a pride in their unit or they will cease to act. I know the case of one company which this year had two officers and six non-commissioned officers to command two men, one of whom was the cook. The captain of that company, Captain Rolston, is one of the best militiamen I know, enthusiastic and able. Never before has he failed to bring out a full company of excellent physique. He told me that he had worked harder than usual at recruiting this year, with this disheartening result, and I believe that one more such experience will drive him from the force. The trouble works both up and down. A non-commissioned officer with no men to command loses interest in his work, and the colonel of a regiment which has dwindled to the size of a fair, company loses heart and keenness, which I know to my sorrow.
And now for the figures In No. 1 district there is an establishment of cavalry, infantry, and army medical corps, of 3,611 officers and men, exclusive of the city corps, and of these only 1,248 attended camp; just barely one-third. In No. 2 district there is an infantry strength of 3,677 officers and men, exclusive of the city corps, and of these only 1,570, far less than half found their way to camp. Startling as these figures are they do not represent the full significance of the case, for not only are we reduced to a minimum in numbers, but the physique of those whom we do get out is anything but satisfactory. Those going to camp under present conditions may be roughly divided into two classes-the enthusiasts, than whom it would be hard to find a better lot, and a large residue who may fairly be described as the fifty cent men, a class not worth even that pittance, men who break the hearts of the good soldiers with whom they are associated, and who are brought out by captains in sheer despair to maintain even the semblance of a company. And here Sir, I cannot refrain from telling of an amusing incident closely connected with the physique of the men which occurred recently at camp Niagara. The inspecting officer was going round a company, and he found fault as to the age of several veterans whose Fenian Raid medals and leathery mahogany skin betokened advanced years. Reaching the other flank of the company he happened on a number of downy youths who must have barely escaped the nursery to be present, and again his strictures broke forth. The captain of the company listened in respectful silence till his superior officer was through, and then remarked, " what

you say is no doubt all true sir, but the average age would be about right." Now Sir, I have given you the figures of these two districts, all that are at present available to me, but inasmuch as these are always much above the average, it is fair to argue that this lamentable state of affairs will be reproduced throughout the Dominion. It may be said that inasmuch as only parts of companies were called out the figures I have quoted are hardly fair, because, had the full numbers been summoned, the total turn out would have been much larger. This cannot, however, be the case. If on calling out but a fraction we have been unable to furnish even that part, then to call out more would produce no more. Having, as I firmly believe, established the danger beyond perad-venture, I now come to the remedy, which in my opinion is an increase of fifty cents a day for every man in the force, exclusive of officers, and an annual drill for the whole establishment. At first blush this may seem a rather ambitious scheme, but the expense between the present and the proposed rate is nothing like as great as many imthis House imagine. The total number of the militia, exclusive of the permanent force, of which I shall speak hereafter, is only 40,151, and figuring the officers at about eight per cent of the whole, or 3,212, we have 36,946 rank and file to whom my proposition applies. To give to each of these an increase of fifty cents a day for the twelve days during which the militia is annually under pay would be six dollars per man, or a total increase of $221,673, just four cents per head of the population of Canada. It is contended by some that a further allowance of 50 cents a day should be made for the horses of the cavalry and field artillery. I have not the exact number of horses to which this increase would apply, but I know that the amount involved added to the $221,673 would still total less than a quarter of a million, which is less than the annual expense of the Halifax garrison maintained for about three years, which has just recently been disbanded, and the saving arising from which may very well be applied to this necessary object. And to whom would the money go ? Not to great corporations or to railway or manufacturing kings, but to thirty-six thousand odd of the young men of Canada-to men who for years have been keeping up a necessary part of the government of this country at an actual loss to themselves. This matter has been quite misunderstood by many honourable members of this House. I have heard it stated this very session in this very place that to increase the pay meant to double the militia vote. The militia vote this year on the main estimates is $1,777,308, and so far from doubling it we require but an eighth of an increase. If, however, the government thinks this increase for drill too great, I have a further Mr. THOMPSON (Haldimand).
proposition to make, w-hich is to let the increase apply to country corps only. I make this proposition out of no disregard for the city corps, which have my admiration and respect. I served my time in the ranks of a city regiment, the Queen's Own Rifles, of Toronto, and my memories of those days are such as to keep my heart very warm towards the city boys; but conditions are different in their case. The country soldier leaves home for twelve days, and is during that time entirely dissociated from his usual avocation. The city soldier does his drill at night, after his day's wage has been earned, and at no loss and but little inconvenience. The country soldier on his return home gets no further privilege or profit from his association with the militia. The city soldier is the year round furnished with a commodious club yclept an armoury. Recognizing these facts, the city soldier in almost every ease does not touch a cent of his pay, but turns it all in to the regimental fund. The question of pay, then, does not seriously affect him. The city corps are not suffering from low pay, but from liability to strike service, which I will discuss briefly later on. Even with the countryman at a dollar a day and.the city man at fifty cents, I believe the former would cost the exchequer slightly less than the latter. Say that the armoury at Halifax cost $300,000, though as a fact I understand it cost quite largely in excess of that amount, and charge that up at six per cent for interest, repairs, and sinking fund-though here again I err by underestimate, for six per cent is not enough. Leaving it at that, however, the annual cost is $18,000. The establishment of the garrison using that armoury is 1,492; therefore each member of it costs for armoury accommodation for the twelve days per annum the sum of one dollar, which, added to his fifty cents, makes a total of $1.50. The armoury of my own regiment is an old frame building somewhat repaired of late, but which could be entirely rebuilt for $2,000. The number of men using that drill shed-it is very properly called a shed and not an armoury-is 367. Figuring on the same basis as that of the Halifax armoury, we find an annual charge of $120, and so each member of the 37th costs for armoury accommodation a little less than three cents a day. Add this to the dollar I propose should be given, and the country soldier costs $1.03 a day as against $1.50(^ for the city man drawing 50-eent pay, in both cases eliminating the cost of clothing/ and equipment, which should be practically the same. In this calculation, Sir, I may have chosen the extremes for comparison. I believe I have, but you will notice that there is the large difference of forty-seven cents per man per day still to play upon. Let me take a less marked case. The Armoury at Brockville cost $40,000. and is used by 277 men. These cost then 72 cents per day for armoury accommodation while

under pay, and adding 50 cents for pay the total daily cost per man is $1.22. Next imagine a country drill shed costing $10,000, and a strong flight of imagination is indeed necessary, for I never knew of one approaching that in cost. It would be used by an 8 company regiment, 367 men. On the same basis of calculation the cost for armoury accommodation would be 16 cents per day, which added to the dollar I propose for the countryman would make his total cost $1.16 per day as against $1.22 for the Brock-ville man. If then we take the average cost of city armouries and country drill sheds, and work them out on the same basis as above, I feel sure that the country soldier at a dollar a day is still costing less than the city soldier at fifty cents a day. Wherefore again I say, if there be not enough to go round, raise the pay of the countryman, and no unfairness is done his neighbour. I have already stated that an increase of fifty cents per day per man would amount to $221,673. But suppose we let the pay of the city corps stand as at present. They number 15,757 men; and deducting this from the total strength, we see that to give the rural corps numbering 22,443, without officers, the increase, I propose, would mean a cost of only $134,658, or less than two and one-half cents per head of our population. It is true that two years ago I advocated increased pay on a graded scale. That might have done then, but since that time conditions have entirely changed, and it will not do at all now. It is too slow. Men drawing pay for twelve days in the 365 are not greatly elated at the prospect of getting ten cents per day more for the drill of the year following. An increase of that amount in the North-west Mounted Police or the permanent force amounts to something at the end of the year, but to the twelve-day soldier it has no drawing power.
While on this question of pay, let me once more say a word for the regimental chaplain, even if my advocacy' of his case subjects me to some mild ridicule, as it did in 1901. The chaplain is undoubtedly a great aid to recruiting. Religion has not yet gone out of fashion in rural Canada, and the erroneous idea that camp is a Godless and wicked place has caused many a parent to keep his willing boy at home. To such people the assurance that a chaplain is going along removes the prejudice, and with it the prohibition. And yet the regimental chaplain is treated as an unwelcome guest. He is given no tent accommodation, and has to rely? on the good nature of some brother officer for the very' canvass over his head. He draws not one cent of pay, but, for all that, has his messing to pay for, as also his uniform. I think he should receive a fair allowance, say two dollars a day, and the total would be a mere bagatelle.
Thus far I have been treating of the pay of the non-permanent militia, but now I wish to refer to the permanent force. This body
is not large enough to form a garrison in Canada, nor was it ever intended that it should. It is the teacher, the faculty, so to speak, of the militia. To this end, we require in its ranks good officers and good men as instructors. With regard to the former, we may consider ourselves fortunate considering the moderate inducements offered, but as to the latter we find that every branch is now far under strength, nor can this be otherwise when the men draw per day rather less than a plumber gets an hour. To my mind, the pay of the regulars must be iucreased. To what extent I shall not attempt to say, feeling less familiar with details here than in the case of the country corps, but the amount could be easily found out by inquiry from the proper sources.
Even with the increased pay, our force will not be on a proper footing unless we drill, as we used to do, every man every year. As I said before, the importance of this is freely admitted by our ministers, who point with pride to the fact that for the six years up to the time that they presented their memorandum to the British government, there had been annual drill for all. If you restrict us to a twelve-day camp, and I believe a longer period, because of the difficulty of getting away from ordinary employment, would be a detriment rather than an advantage, you must not reduce that to six days a year by making it twelve days every other year.
A great deal of unnecessary trouble was caused this year by withholding notice for camp until within from three weeks to ten days of the time ordered. Knowing that some regiments were not to be called out, a feeling of uncertainty pervaded the whole, and I can assure you that recruiting is too unpleasant a job to be undertaken on chances. When the summons did come, it was found that some of the best regiments had been overlooked. Of these some few were afterwards added to the list of the fortunate, but at so late a date as to give them totally inadequate time for preparation. One colonel of a belated regiment arrived in camp with seven out of eight companies, and he informed me that his eighth captain did not know yet that the regiment had been ordered out. Still another regiment, knowing itself to be amongst the most efficient, was preparing for camp as a matter of course, when the list of those chosen appeared and its name was not there. Subsequently, but at the last moment, it was added. Had it not been, I have it on good authority, that every officer in the corps would have sent in his resignation. Why are we put to these unnecessary inconveniences, when our burdens are already so heavy to bear ? We are told that parliament had not voted the money. Then let parliament hereafter vote it in time to give every one concerned not less than three months' notice. Better still, let it be the pronounced policy of the government to drill every man

every year, and the uncertainty will entirely disappear.
Recruiting has still further been injured by leaving the regimental bands at home. Nothing is more attractive to the average individual than good band music, and with the soldier this is especially the case. The great armies of Europe have not eliminated the band-the sword may have to go, but the big drum, never.
