The strength of a band is limited to three men per company, and as these have to put in their rifle practice with the rest, and take part in all marches as well, we can see that they are not a mere luxury, but soldiers like the rest. When next year we go out, as I am sure we shall once more in full strength, let the band head our columns as of yore.
I shall now take up the danger threatening our city corps from their frequent employment for the protection of property during strikes. When a large strike is on it almost always follows that lawlessness results, and while I would be far from asserting that any large percentage of our labouring classes are bent, under such circumstances, upon destruction, the fact remains that there are always some who put in danger valuable property. To meet these men the militia is invariably invoked. Now, the young man who enters the militia does so from patriotic motives, to defend his country in case of war, perhaps with the hope of seeing active service far afleld in the empire's cause, but for one thing he certainly dees not join, that is to be a cheap policeman. Take, on the one hand, the average office man called out for several days to protect property. If his employer does not actually dismiss him at the time, he gives him a fair warning that he will certainly do so if it ever occurs again. Nor is it quite fair to rise in righteous indignation and attack the employer who takes this course as a grasping man and an unpatriotic citizen. It not infrequently happens that a number of men in a large office belong to some military organization ; *fti'tknt case, or even where one belongs, if he be the trusted man in some particular line of the business, disorganization, with its attendant heavy loss, is sure to follow, and we are all alike very anxious to avoid the least injury to that very tender part of our anatomy-the pocket. This being the case, how can we expect any employer to submit without complaint to inconvenience and loss entailed in the suppression of some strike, a matter which excites no man's patriotism, a matter in which sympathy may even be with the strikers themselves.
Next take the case of the other main source of strength to city corps, the artisan, and in what a position does he And himself when called out on strike duty, in many cases directly opposed to his personal chums, to the members of Iiis own union. The result of all this is that recruiting is becoming increasingly difficult

in the cities, and some other means must be devised to meet the case.
A solution has been suggested in the employment of the permanent force, at least in all cases where the strikes are prolonged. The idea is not without merit, but must for all that be greatly modified if fairness to the men is to be maintained. To take permanent soldiers from place to place on strike duty under existing conditions would be unfair in the extreme. In their case too the men enlisted to be soldiers, and not a reserve for the police. They should not be asked to do such duty for their current rate of pay, whether in the future that be increased or not, but when doing policeman's work they should get constable's pay, or at .east near it. In this case surely we can afford to be generous, since the city employing llieni would have to foot the bill, and so there would be no increase in the militia burdens of the country. I think I know Tommy Atkins quite well enough to assert that if tills special pay were forthcoming he would be only too glad to serve as often as called on. More than that I am satisfied that the same amount of work could be done by a much smaller force of permanent soldiers. Their presence would overawe a mob more than ten times the number of volunteers every second man of whom was known personally by the rioters. Their discipline would be fully equal to any call made upon it, and knowing this the crowd would not go to such lengths as with their fellow-citizens for the time being fitted out in soldier's clothes.
With regard to the rifle clubs organized within the past few years, I would like to speak shortly. The membership in these now amounts to about 20,000. As many of these clubs are, however, military, and as in many of the civilian clubs, several members also belong to the active militia, we must greatly reduce this number if we would get at the value of the asset as a source of reinforcement in time of war. I do not think we would be placing it too low if we stated the number of rifle club men outside the force at about 10,000. There is undoubtedly cause of congratulation in this good beginning, but I must say we have no right to look upon it as anything but a beginning. That a proportion of 1 in 550 of our population is enrolled in these organizations is hardly sufficient. I have already explained the skeleton system on which our militia is organized. To fill the various corps up to war strength we would require about 80,000 men, and as these, even if trained rifle shots, would still be very green for the purpose of soldiering, surely they should not be more unfit still by knowing nothing of the rifle. Of the members of the clubs moreover many would be physically unfit for service, so that to get our 80,000 we should have at least a total of 100,000 to choose from or just ten times the number now enrolled. I think that there

is plenty of willingness in all parts of Canada to join rifle clubs, but what we lack in many localities is leaders to undertake the organization required in forming nil association. When business organizations seek to extend their operations they send men on the road to solicit customers. 1 think this is entirely a business proposition, and it seems to me that we could not spend a few thousand dollars better than in putting from ten to twenty smart young fellows from the permanent corps out to work up clubs of this kind. These emissaries could have a proper knowledge too of the suitability of certain localities for ranges, and could make reports on the same. The cost to the country for each member of a club is so insignificant, that we should avail ourselves of the opportunity to increase our resisting strength while adding but little to our tax burdens.
A cognate subject is that of cadet corps. Their spread is very gratifying, and I congratulate the minister on the assistance he is giving them. Here again we can get a great deal at little expense. A boy learns quickly, and what he learns in boyhood lie remembers. The school teacher simply adds drill to the subjects in which he gives instruction, and no expense is incurred on his part. The amount -to arm and equip the boys is not very great, and the practice with miniature ball cartridge teacnes a great deal at a minimum of cost. The hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) has said that he fears we are encouraging overmuch the military spirit of the youth of our country. I cannot agree with him. I am satisfied that for half a century to come the opportunities in civil life in Canada will be so great as compared with anything a soldier can hope for, that the whole difficulty will be as it is at present, getting a reasonable amount of military duty done, not in a rage for militarism. More than that I believe that drill in our schools is an excellent thing for the boys, both physically and morally. As to the former, it makes the youths stand up straight and relieves them from the student's hump that is so destructive to the proper development of the organs of the chest, and as to the latter the discipline develops good manners and clean living. I am quite aware that education is a matter for the provinces, and that it is only by co-operation with them that anything along the line of a general introduction of drilling in the schools can be achieved, but I understand that in most cases they are willing to meet the federal government half-way, and, in fact, they have already done so in numerous instances. The Minister of Militia is certainly to be congratulated upon the progress he is making in the formation of the various departmental services, of which a few years ago we had absolutely none.
The army medical staff and corps are fast reaching an efficiency which is most gratifying to us all. It does seem, Sir, that
when medical men put their shoulder to the wheel they do so with a will, and this has been no exception to the rule. Some of the brightest doctors and surgeons have cast in their lot with this branch of the service, and in case of trouble the sick and wounded would be looked after under the very best modern conditions. Then we take the engineers. Many of us had an oppor-tuity of seeing the splendid work done by the Toronto company at the recent horse show there, and were delighted with it all. Perhaps the best feature of that unit is that It is composed of School of Practical Science men. These, after their course, scatter all over Canada, and each in turn becomes, if necessary, an instructor, with the apt Cana-dain handy-man as a pupil. The body is of incalculably more value for this very reason, than if composed of city men only, who would for the most part live and die in that particular locality.
The latest notable addition to our militia is the army service corps. In campaigning the handling of stores is a good half the battle, and we are now getting in a position to use the splendid natural resources we have in farmers' horses and wagons, &c. Under the superintendence of that hard working and excellent officer, Lieutenant Colonel Bigger, the organization is advancing rapidly. In our last camp we had the army service corps with us for the first time. They slaughtered our cattle for us, and never before did our men enjoy such good meat rations. Next camp, I understand, all the baking of bread will also be done by these all round handy fellows. While on the subject of rations, I wish to say a word of thanks on behalf of the men for thf new scale, the greater variety it supplies, &c. The food in camp all round this year was excellent, and if, as we expect, the present standard be kept up, one of the main grievances which deterred fellows from going into camp will be removed.
Then there is now being organized an intelligence department and corps of guides, a most useful and necessary body, but on none of these matters will I enlarge, as the minister will no doubt give us a full account at a later date. The school of musketry, however, must not be passed over. I hear it very favourably spoken of far and near, and only a few days ago an officer who had served twice in South Africa told me that on returning to Canada he had taken the course, and found it most useful. He spoke of the indefatigable work being done by Colonel Cartwright, and pronounced this whole thing as the most useful move that had been made for years in the militia.
The very creation, however, of all these subsidiary services, if I may so call them, calls for the continuation of the main body whose handmaidens they are. In times past we had the men and not the equipment, arms, and services, are we now to find our-

selves with gcod services organized, with plentiful arms and clothing, and without the men ? Or has the time not come, this time so ably described by the Minister of Finance as the times of prosperous Canadian finance, when we can afford to have both men and their complement at one and the same time in reasonable number ?
Sir, I have finished my remarks. I have striven to give credit where credit was due, and to point out dangers where they, In my opinion, existed. I have carefully kept politics out of my speech as I trust other gentlemen will do when treating of militia subjects, and which I always propose to do unless forced Into another course by dissimilar conduct on their part. I believe that better days are yet in store for us, and that this government will yet spend the moderate sums I have mentioned to preserve to Canada the main part of her fine militia force.

I think that speech is too good, and the subject too important and too well presented, not to require some observations from the ministerial benches. I do not say this as a military man, because that is not in my line, and it may be considered presumptuous on my part to say anything on the subject, even at the risk of being unpopular. I must compliment the hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. Thompson) on the very clear and able way he has presented his case, because I think he has made out a very good and a very strong case. But I must draw attention to the fact that I think he was a little remiss in not giving notice that he intended to bring this question before the House, so that some more members of the government might have been present, especially the Minister of Militia, to hear this able speech. I noticed that during the greater part of his speech there were only two Ministers of the Crown present), supplemented by another one who came in towards the close. I think it was too good a speech not to reach them, but I am afraid they are so busy with the affairs of state that they will hardly take time to read it in ' Hansard.'
If they get no summer holidays.

He drew a painful picture of what our boasted militia have come to during all these years while the present government have been endeavouring to improve it in every direction and to make it what we all desire it should be. I do not think it is creditable to the government, or creditable to the militia either. If we hope to keep up a force in Canada that will be of any service to the country or of any value to the British empire, we must do much better than we have been doing heretofore. There was one thing I asked myself while the hon. member was speaking.' When he Mr. THOMPSON (Haldimand).
gave us his description of what the present militia force was, he said it was ' fast crumbling into disintegration, and decay, and disorganization,' 'that it was only a shadow of a skeleton to-day.' That seems to be very much like the similia similibus c-urantur morbi species of practice, that is infinitesimal doses. I was going to say that it has degenerated down to homeopathy. It is said that Halmemam, the celebrated practitioner who first described the homeopathic treatment of disease, decided that you must reduce medicine to about the sixtieth dilution to get the most beneficial effects possible for the human body when diseased. Now, if that be the case, I must say that the Minister of Militia seems to be a patron of that idea, for he has endeavoured to dilute the militia down to that extent that it is to-day only a shadow of a skeleton. It was said in describing what homeopathic soup is that you take a chicken that has starved to death, you drive a stake in the ground, and you hang the chicken up in such a position in the open air that the shadow of the stake can shine on the boiling pot, and after boiling it for half an hour in that way you have homeopathic soup. I should think the government have been feeding the militia on homeopathic doses, and treating them to about the same regimen for the last two or three years, otherwise it could not have degenerated into the shadow of a skeleton, as the hon. member admits it has to-day. While he was speaking I was wondering whether the hon. member's county had voted twenty-five cents a day as additional pay for militia men for the present year.
My county did not, and I never asked my county to do so, and I never will. It is not their place.

I agree with him there. But we know that many counties do that, and because the government do not provide sufficient pay, they supplement it by the paltry sum of twenty-five cents a day. I do not think any county should be compelled to do that, I think this country is wealthy enough to pay the men reasonably well without county councils being obliged to supplement the pay by a further amount. I notice that the amount voted in the militia estimates this year is $1,766,000. Now, it was stated that the men, instead of getting fifty cents a day, ought to get $1 a day, and I confess that I think they should. I do not think that any young man should be expected to go out and put in his time on drill unless he got at least $1 a day. There may be something in his enthusiasm and in his desire to have an outing, but all that is short of what is required to induce young men to take that interest in the militia force which they should take. An additional fifty cents a day, as I figure it up-I think they usually put in fifteen days drill.
Twelve.

To give that additional amount it would require $200,000. Surely this country can afford to give $200,000 more, and particularly to the rural corps because they appear to be poorly paid. There is not that excitement or enthusiasm associated with the rural corps which surrounds the city corps or the eclat that attends military life in cities and there is not the same inspiration or stimulus to the young men of the country as there is to the young men of the cities. I think the government might give that additional amount and pay these young men what they should be paid. I, for one, though not a military man, have never objected to this. I have always said that I believed that the proper thing to do was to pay our young men reasonably well, because if they ever hope to make them of any value they must be kept up to the highest standard of excellence and you cannot do that when you starve them iu pay and rations. I am glad to hear that there has been some improvement in the rations. I think the government might go one better and improve their pay as well. I regret the Minister of Militia and Defence (Sir Frederick Borden) is not present to hear what has been said to-night. We have a general officer commanding to give us advice as to what should be done and we have advice coming from various sources, but I think one of the most important things to be done in the interest of the militia is to see that the pay is increased beyond the amount at which it is placed at the present time.

Mr. Speaker, I want to say a few words upon this question. I only heard the latter part of the remarks of the hon. member for Haldimand and Monck (Mr. Thompson), but if the first part of his speech was as good as the last, I am sorry to have missed any of it. The hon. gentleman's speech is different from the speeches that used to be heard in this parliament ten or fifteen years ago. The hon. member for Haldimand represents young Canadians who will in a few years dominate the public opinion of Canada. I see it growing on every hand, and it is the public opinion that should have dominated Canada thirty years ago. But, were Conservative ministers of militia met in the past ? Every vote that was brought down was opposed by narrow men who never looked an inch beyond their noses. In that way the whole public life of Canada has been narrowed and degraded. How differently we now treat hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House. Here I am in the interest of Canada doing all I can to strengthen the public opinion of this country. I am willing to do it and then I am willing to take the chance of going out into the country and beating hon. gentlemen opposite, because, I say, we are more
liberal-minded than they and we can out-Herod them in the game of broad politics.
I want to say one word about militarism. We hear an hon. gentleman in a high position in this country going around and talking about militarism. It is said that a country that is caught by catch words is a very ignorant country. The masses of the United States used to be caught by such a cry as ' Tippecanoe and Tyler too.' Some cry like that would elect a president of the United States against the most logical argument that could be advanced, because, at that time the people of the United States were untrained to think, untrained to understand the issue of public life and of public policy. To the people of England, of Germany and of France, such a catch cry as ' a cheaploaf,' or some nonsense like that, will appeal more forcibly than the most logical argument that could be adduced. Any hon. gentleman who undertakes to talk militarism in this country is simply stamping himself as a demagogue. There is no room for militarism in Canada. You must have a besotted and ignorant population before you can have militarism. You must have an army taken from the masses of the people who are ignorant. Then, you must have these ignorant people controlled day by day and you must have them under surveillance because they are unable to govern themselves. The people of Canada are a self-governing people. The people of Canada pursue occupations which make men of them. Every Canadian is more or less of a soldier in the civilized life of the country. A man is called to be a banker in the morning, he is required to be a constitutional lawyer in the afternoon, he is required to be a parliamentarian, he is required perhaps to be a mechanic, an agriculturist or a gardener ; in short, he embraces all the qualities that go to make a well-trained man. His mind is trained, his intellect is alert, his body is alert and the result is that all we want in this country is a fortnight or three weeks training. There is nothing the men of Canada want more than a month's training to be more than equal to holding our owu against the trained bands of Europe. When any man gets up in this country and talks about militarism he fancies that the people are uncultivated and ignorant and that a catchword of that kind will take the place of a sound argument. We do not want militarism in this country, but what we do want is an undaunted martial spirit, the spirit of a brave people and you only can get that by having something of chivalry in the military life of the country. Every people that have dominated the world have been a martial people, an undaunted people, a people of pride and martial feeling will not only bear us triumphant in every war, but it will make us triumphant in manufactures and the arts of peace. Therefore, I was pleased to hear the speech that was made by the hon. mem-

ber for Haldimand and Monck and to know that a just sum of money would be voted for the militia of this country in order that a martial spirit may prevail. I am proud every time the militia go out in my county. We have a splendid day in Colchester wThen the militia are called out. When the band strikes up our boys run out to see their neighbour boys going out to be trained. The day is looked upon as a gala day and it stimulates that feeling of self-reliance, courage and pluck that makes men assume the duty of being soldiers and of being trained to protect their country in time of need. Consequently, I am pleased with the state of affairs presented here to-night and I simply rose to say that what we want is a martial spirit in this country and I hope ministers of the Crown on the other side will not go around talking about militarism, because it is a degradation of public life to hear a minister engaging in any such nonsense.

speakername: The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Hon. W. S. Fielding).

speechtext:
I merely want to say one or two words in regard to what has fallen from my hon. friend from Haldimand (Mr. Thompson), who has presented the subject to the House to-night in a very clear and interesting way. At the commencement of his observations the hon. gentleman (Mr. Thompson) was somewhat enthusiastic about these w'ords which appear in the memorandum presented by the Canadian ministers at the colonial conference, concerning defence. He cited the words :
If defects exist there is every desire on the part of the Canadian government to remove them and for this purpose the advice and assistance of experienced imperial officers will be welcome in all reasonable efforts made to secure an efficient system.
I would hardly be prepared to join in the enthusiasm of my hon. friend with regard to that expression, because I do not know exactly what else the government could have said :
If defects exist there is every desire on the part of the Canadian government to remove them.
I would look upon that as a remarkably guarded phrase, and I should be inclined to think that the government could adopt any policy it saw fit after having used language of that kind, which excited so much the commendation of my hon. friend from Haldimand.
However, the speech of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Thompson) must be regarded as a very severe arraignment of the government with regard to its militia policy. There is no possible reason for attaching any other import to them. The position of matters is, that SI.000.000 was voted for militia purposes in 1890 and during the present year we have a vote of one and three quarter millions nearly ; yet my hon. friend, on his responsibility as a member of this House, and as an officer of the very highest rank in Canada, tells us that if the demoralization and disorganization which have been going on for the past two years shall continue for a very short time longer, the militia force in Canada will be practically non-existent. My hon. friend from Grey (Mr. Sproule) referred to this language, but he hardly did justice to it.
No body could do justice to it.	-

My hon. friend from Haldimand has told us that the militia force as called out is not even the skeleton of a skeleton, but merely the shadow of the skeleton of a skeleton. As he himself said, it would be impossible to use any stronger language as to our militia force. If there is every desire on the part of the Canadian

government to remove defects, and if this disorganization and demoralization liave been going on for two years, as the hon. gentleman (Mr. Thompson) says, it does seem to me that some reply should be made by the government at a very early date to the charge which is brought against it in this respect. 1 appreciate the fact that the Minister of Militia is necessarily absent to-night, and that my hon. friend the Minister' of Finance cannot be expected to deal with a matter which is not concerned with his own department- particularly in view of the fact that the duties of his department are very onerous-but I do think that the presentment of this case by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Thompson) calls for the earliest answer on the part of the government. And in view of the statements made by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Thompson) I do not know how a very satisfactory explanation or answer can be given by the government. If the militia force of Canada can be brought up to an efficient standard by increasing the pay as the hon. gentleman suggests, I do not think that there is any man in this House who would not be prepared to support such a measure, if it really would accomplish the results which he hopes for. But possibly there may be some question as to that. My hon. friend (Mr. Thompson) has adverted to the fact that the wages are very high at the present time, that men are busy in other occupations, and as I understood his remarks, he attributes the falling off of recruiting to these facts. However, there may be some question as to whether the remedy which he proposes would be sufficient to bring our militia up to the standard which he thinks is a sufficient one. But if the House could be persuaded that the proper strength could be obtained by a measure of that kind, I do not think that many hon. gentlemen in the House would be prepared to say that the government would not be justified in adopting the course which the hon. gentleman has suggested. I agree entirely with my hon. friend when he says that -we do not want any spirit of militarism in this country
The member for Colchester (Mr. Gourley) wall not allow such a declaration.

I understood the remarks of my hon. friend (Mr. Gourley) in an entirely different sense from that which seems to have impressed itself on my hon. friend from Labelle (Mr. Bourassa). My hon. friend (Mr. Gourley) said that he for one would be opposed to the spirit of militarism in Canada, and he thought it was absolutely impossible that such a spirit should exist in this country.
Hear, hear.

What my hon. friend (Mr. Gourley) said was that he did
desire to see in Canada a martial spirit; that is a spirit of courage, a spirit which would induce us to resist any oppression from a foreign country. In fact I think he might have used the motto of the volunteers in England fifty years ago : Defence not defiance. It was in that way I understood the remarks of my hon, friend (Mr. Gourley).
Hear, hear ; they could not be misunderstood.

It is perhaps to be regretted that my hon. friend from Haldimand (Sir. Thompson) had not the opportunity of bringing up this matter when there was a larger attendance in the House, and when the Minister of Militia would be present. I have no doubt that when the minister returns and when those military gentlemen are present, there may be an opportunity to discuss this matter more fully. I have merely risen at the present time to say that the hon. member for Haldimand is to be congratulated on the very clear way in which he has presented his case to the House to-night, and I think that the case he has presented is one which demands a very early answer indeed from the administration, because the case made out-if the statements are to be taken as correct-is certainly one which is not complimentary to the government.

At the risk of falling short of the standard of patriotism which has been determined by the member for Colchester, I must say that I entirely disagree with the position which has been placed before us by the member for Haldimand. I do not dispute that the hon. gentleman is, of course, well versed on the subject of the state of the militia, which I am not; but I say that if with the present expenditure on militia matters, our militia is not in good condition, then the only remedy which I see for it is that the strength of our militia force should be reduced, and not the expenditure increased.
Would my hon. friend (Mr. Bourassa) reduce the force below the shadow of the skeleton of a skeleton ?

When I see such military men as my hon. friend (Mr. Thompson) and other members of this House who do not at all look like the skeleton of a skeleton, I am inclined to think that the metaphor is altogether too strong. It would appear, however, that the chief defect in the organization is as to numbers. I was not here when the hon. member (Mr. Thompson) spoke, but I understand that he quoted me as an authority, and said that I was in favour of an increase in the expenditure on militia.

If I may be allowed a word in explanation, I may say that I did use the hon. gentleman's name

in his absence. I said I felt much encouraged by the sentiments to which he had given utterance. As a matter of fact, it was in his speech on the address in reply to the speech from the Throne, in which he said he would like to see the militia put on a proper basis, and for one he was quite willing to take over the defence of Halifax and Esquimalt, which I may state would cost ten times as much as X am asking to put the militia on a proper basis.

It is not so much the figure that I am criticising, as the spirit and the prinicple of the suggestion. I am not in favour of inducing the young men of this country to enter the militia. For those who have a taste and vocation to enter the militia, well and good. Let them enter the militia, and take it as it is. If the present pay is not sufficient to induce a sufficient number of good men to enter the militia, then I repeat, let the number be reduced and the pay be increased. If it is a good thing to develop the martial spirit in this country, it is also a good thing to keep our common sense, and it is perfectly foolish for any common-sense citizen to suppose that by increasing our militia by 20,000 or 50,000 men, we would improve our military position. It is perfectly ridiculous to have more men than are required to keep order in this country. Sly hon. friend resented the suggestion that our militia should be called on to do police work in this country. Those who attended the coronation did not like it very well when the British authorities called upon them to do police work in the streets of London, but I do not see why they should resent having to do police work in Canada for the purpose of making the laws of Canada respected after being called to do police work in London to keep the rowdies at a distance from the English aristocracy. But so far as external defence is concerned, I repeat that we should not lose our heads. To prepare for withstanding an attack from a European country is out of the question.
The new navy will protect us on the seaport.

I am not much more enthusiastic for the navy under the control of my hon. friend the Minister of Marine than I am for an army under the control of the absent Minister of Militia. If we are ever called upon to organize this country upon a military footing, it will only be required by our situation in America. So long as we are situated as at present-perhaps this opinion may not correspond to the martial spirit to which my hon. friend from Colchester (Mr. Gourley) has appealed-but I think our greatest and only safeguard against foreign invasion from any European country is the neighbourhood of the United States-much more than any defence from our own forces-much more even than any defence from the British empire.
Oh, hold on.

I admit that this is not satisfactory to the high spirit of my hon. friend from Colchester. But we have to take the facts as they are, and this has been stated and acknowledged up to the last few years, before we grew to be such big people, especially in military matters. But so long as we are not a big people in poxmlation and in wealth, I do not think we should aim too much to be a big people in other things; it will not lead to much result. So far as attacks from the United States are concerned, as long as the hon. member for Colchester and his family are there, he has promised us that he will resist these attacks and even go to Washington. But the existence of the hon. member for Colchester is not eternal, and it may be that many Canadians are not willing to go to the trenches and even to Washington. The average people of this country, who have their own conception of patriotism, think it is foolish for the people of Canada to imagine that they can organize upon a military footing to resist a nation of SO,000,000 people in our neighbourhood. Therefore, so long as we are not in a position to organize to withstand an attack from the United States, I think it is perfectly foolish to increase our military expenditure. I must beg pardon of the House if I refer to a past debate; but since the hon. member for Haldimand has done it, I repeat what I said at the beginning of this session, let our militia be in number just what is necessary to maintain order in the different provinces of Canada, and let it be organized on a proper basis. Let our officers be properly trained, and let our soldiers be properly drilled, but no increase in the pay should take place until the number is reduced to what it should be. I have heard members of this House who are interested in military matters defend the policy of the British government and of this government in inducing young men who come from our military college at Kingston to enter the British army. I have already protested, and I still protest against that policy. If we want to have a proper militia force and a proper permanent force in Canada, I think it is foolish on our part to let the British authorities come here and offer commissions to the best young men who graduate from our military school, and deprive our militia and our permanent force of their services. We have organized a military school at Kingston for the benefit of the people of Canada, to train officers for the Canadian military force; and it is perfectly ridiculous to speak of the defence of Canada when we allow a foreign government-and in this respect the English government is a foreign government-to take the pick of our young men after they have been educated at the expense of the people of Canada, and place them in the British army. If we are going to have a Canadian militia, let it be Cana-

dian ; let it be what is required for this country, and nothing more. It is all very well to speak of a martial spirit and all that, but it is equally well to keep our common sense.

I regret not having been present when the hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. Thompson) addressed the House on military matters. I regard that hon. gentleman, from his wide experience, as being able to speak intelligently on this subject. As one who has listened to military discussions in this House for fourteen sessions, I must admit that the militia of this country has suffered in consequence of the inexperience in militia matters of members who have discussed subjects of that character; and I am bound to say that a few of us who have taken more interest in military matters than others- though I regret to say that I am not a military man myself-are placed at a disadvantage by reason of the course pursued by the Minister of Militia during this session. First we had in the speech from the Throne an announcement of the intention of the government to introduce a Militia Act. That is abandoned, I understand, and the wrongs and weaknesses of our present Militia Act are still to continue, though many of those wrongs and weaknesses have been pointed out from time to time to the Minister of Militia. It has been customary for the heads of the various departments when submitting their estimates, to lay before this House their policy. We find that course not pursued on this occasion in militia matters. We find the minister deferring his statement until he brings down his supplementary estimates. That is placing many of us at a great disadvantage, and is besides a slap in the face to the officer commanding the militia, because I find in his report that he had submitted another and a special report to the Minister of Militia containing certain proposals which, if adopted, would add to the efficiency of the militia. If my hon. friend from Haldimand is correct, our militia are fast falling into a condition of decay, which makes it all the more necessary that these proposals, which the major general recommends for the purpose of improving our militia, should be before the House. But we. are told that we cannot have this special report, but must wait until the dying days of the session, when the hon. minister chooses to make his statement. My hon. friend from Haldimand (Mr. Thompson) suggests that we should increase the pay of the rural corps, which would involve an expenditure in the neighbourhood of a quarter million dollars. We have something like $1,166,000 asked for in the main estimates, and the hon. minister proposes to bring down a very large item in his supplementaries, so that it will be seen that our expenditure on militia is by no means inconsiderable ; and such being the case, we are entitled to all the information
possible which will enable us to intelligently discuss this question.
The hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bour-assa), who never misses an opportunity to criticise and disparage our militia force, referred, in a sneering manner, to the hon. member for Colchester (Mr. Gourley) as being one of our Canadian bulwarks, and one who would resent an attack by the United States. Well, Mi'. Speaker, I believe that the hon. member for Colchester would, even if he were the only man to do so, resist any attack from the neighbouring republic, but I regret to say that I am not able to pay the same compliment to the hon. member for Labelle. In fact, I believe that he would rather defend an attack than resist it.
I do not think that in times of peace we should neglect putting our militia forces on the best possible basis. The time of peace is the proper time to prepare for war. If you have a good defence, that will go a long way to prevent any attack. I have no desire to say anything more than to strongly condemn the course followed by the Minister of Militia in not furnishing this House with all the information necessary to enable us to intelligently discuss the militia estimates.

I do not agree, Mr. Speaker, at all with the hon. member for Haldfmand (Mr. Thompson). I do not share in the ideas he has expressed. In my opinion, if the government were to follow his advice, the result would be the ruin of our government and our country. I do not think I can better make clear my point than by taking a homely illustration. A man, for instance, has a son to whom, when he reaches a certain age, he makes the gift of a colt. The colt is broken in, and then requires a harness and a buggy and a whip. Then it will not do to leave that colt idling in the stable, but the young man must drive it out, and as he drives out he meets other young men on the road in other rigs, and occasionally he will stop at a hotel and have a drink with his friends, and leave the colt standing while he is enjoying himself inside. The result is that both the colt and the young man are ruined. The same thing would happen if we were to raise an army such as the hon. member for Haldimand speaks of. Here is a country to the south of us with a population of eighty million people. In the two states of New York and Pennsylvania there are more people than in this whole Dominion. That country is the only one we have to fear, and I say frankly that if the United States should take the notion of invading Canada, they will do so in spite of Canada and all England.
No.

Yes, they will. Suppose you were to raise an army here of 30,000 or 40,000 men, what would that be against

the United States ? It would not be a drop in the bucket. Whenever the Americans take it into their heads to come over, they will come in spite of anybody and everybody. If we raise an army, we will be like the young man with his colt. We will have to make use of our soldiers just to see how good they are, just to show the world how well they can fight, and the result will be that we will be wiped out, and that is all we will get for all our expenditure. I say let well enough alone. Go through this country from house to house, and you will scarcely see a gun or a rifle or a revolver, but travel through the states, and evex-ywhere you go you will hardly find a family which has not two or three guns in the house. I have been in their houses, especially in the rebel states, and in many of these houses, where they had no bread, I have seen three guns hanging from the wall. I am talking from experience, and I would like to know what we could do if we fell into the hands of such a people. We have quite enough soldiers, and my advice is to let well enough alone. To have more soldiers would entail more expense, and we are spending quite enough already on the militia.

I wish to congratulate the hon. member for Haldi-mand (Mr. Thompson), not so much on the clever manner in which he pi'esented his case, as on his courage in presenting it. It requires some courage on the part of a private member to offer what may be considered a criticism of the administration which he supports. That is not a frequent occurrence in the House, and that makes it all the more creditable to the hon. gentleman who takes this course. It is right and proper that a member of this parliament, on whatever side he may be, should offer criticism from his place when he finds it necessary ; and I regret that in this instance, instead of my hon. friend being supported in the position he takes by the other side of the House, instead of tlie debate being pursued from the strictly non-partisan standpoint from which he spoke, his criticisms are at once made use of for party attack. Let me say that the government is not so open to attack on this point as is the opposition, whose duty it is to criticise and to put before the country the shoi'tcomings of the government where-ever any exist. There is a certain condition of affairs existing in regard to the'militia force. The hon. member for Haldimand says the pay is too low. The pay is the same as it was ten or fifteen years ago, no more and no less. If it is not enough to-day -and certainly I, for one, say it is not enough, and I am glad we have the endorsa-tion of members of the opposition to the same effect
The members of the opposition are not making it a political matter are they ?
Not to that extent-I give them credit for that.

In what respect are they ?
Mi\ OLIVER. They-well, give me leave to finish my remai'ks. The pay being the same now as it was fifteen or twenty years ago, the l'eason that it is not enough now, when it was enough then, is that the conditions of the country have changed. Now that may not be placed to the credit of the government-it will certainly not be by our friends of the opposition-but I hope they will not blame the government for that change of conditions. As the general question has been discussed let me take the opportunity of offering to the House the views which I hold in regard to military matters and militarism. A voluntary organization, such as we have and hope to maintain, is the very opposite of militarism, as I understand the word. A system whereby the citizens of the country voluntarily band themselves together for the purpose of fitting themselves to defend the country in time of danger is entirely different from the system under which they are forced to take service and play the part of soldiers in such proportion to the population as to constitute a backbreaking burden upon the country. That is what I understand as militarism-the condition which prevails in European countries, where the whole population is levied upon, willing or unwilling, and the burden is so great as to cripple the state, financially, commercially and industi-ially. Now it would be a good thing if there was no necessity for soldiers. There may come a time in the history of earth when soldiers will not be necessary. I believe we are taught something to that effect in Sunday school. But the fact is that that time has not arrived. The fact is also that if we would play our part as men, as a nation and as a part of the empire, we must be prepared to hold what we have, even if we have to hold it as soldiers. There is only one way of doing it. As long as we are in the world, we cannot escape responsibilities of human beings. And the history of the world is this-the man or the nation who will not defend their own rights or their own honour very soon are brought into a position of being obliged to defend somebody else's rights and somebody else's honour. We cannot escape from that position and it is our part, as men, to support our place, if God has given us a place, and to support that place with ci'edit and dignity. It has been said that there is no use in our organizing a military force in this country, that we are a small country and a weak country, and that we cannot provide a military force that would be adequate for our purposes. We are about six millions of people and our country is one of the

largest countries in tlie world. We have interests to defend. Then in God's name, what else are we to do but defend those interests 1 And, although in Canada we are only; five or six millions of people, we surely do not forget that we belong to, or, more properly, we are part of, an empire which stretches around the world, and which contains hundreds of millions of loyal subjects who are prepared to shed their blood in all parts of the empire and in all places of the world for the maintenance of what they believe to be their best interests under the empire's flag. If the native of India, a man who is not of the same race or the same religion as ourselves, who knows nothing of our language, if that man, the black man, if you like, is ready to shed his blood for the flag of Britain, surely, we men of Canada of British birth or British descent-or, if you like, of French birth or descent, for I would not say anything so discreditable to a man of the noble race of Fra nee as to say that he would not fight for what he believed to be his rights-it is not for us, surely, to say that we will not take our part as soldiers or as taxpayers in maintaining the integrity of the British empire, which can only be maintained by defending it wherever it may be attacked, be it near or far. I should say, certainly, it would be better to have a smaller number of soldiers and have them better paid, than to have a larger number of soldiers more poorly paid. I do not pretend for an instant that this country can offer to those who are its citizen soldiers an adequate monetary inducement ; but we can certainly offer them an indemnity that will show at least our good will and that will not make an invidious distinction between these men who, when called upon to serve by putting in their drill as volunteers, are ready thus to show their patriotism, and those who stay at home and do not thus show their patriotism. We cannot all turn out and drill as volunteers. Possibly we all don't want to. Some of us are not very ardent military men in our own persons, and of those, I admit, I am one. But I hope I am not such a poltroon, such a coward. I trust 1 am not so unfit to be a citizen of a free country that X am not prepared to pay reasonably and honourably to the man who does sacrifice his time and thereby display his patriotism.

1 should not have i-isen, but that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Oliver) who has just taken his seat, charged that in the discussion which has taken place since we had the pleasure of listening to the admirable speech of the hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. Thompson), gentlemen on this side of the House who have taken part in the discussion have endeavoured to gain party advantage from some of the statements made by that hon. gentleman. I think that such an expression is much to be regretted. I re-180
pudiate the assertion of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Oliver) and 1 invite him to make good the statement he has made that an attempt has been made by hon. gentlemen on this side to seek party advantage or make party capital out of what has been said. I was under the impression that a more sympathetic hearing could not have been given to any hon. gentleman than that which was given by hon. gentlemen who sit on this side to the speech, the splendid speech, the speech so full of information, delivered by the hon. member for Haldimand.
The hon. leader of the opposition took the opportunity of stating that he was in sympathy with the proposition of the hon. member for Haldimand, that if it were necessary to make the militia force efficient, an increase in the pay of militia-men should be given. That does not look as if any party capital was attempted to be made by hon. gentlemen on this side of the House; that rather looks as if they were prepared to anticipate the action of the government in supporting the proposition of the hon. member for Haldimand, and in endorsing his views, as the leader of the opposition did, ill advance of a declaration from the gov-be increased. I take it that when a re-ernment, that the pay of the militia should sponsible member of this House makes the statements that the member for Haldimand has made, that the members of this House would be derelict in their duty, no matter what the consequences might be, if they did not draw attention to them and emphasize these statements as best they could.
The hon. member for Alberta (Mr. Oliver) said that when the present government came into office the pay of the militia was only fifty cents a day. That is the sum they are receiving now. But, he says, conditions have changed. So they have; and what we find fault with in the administration of militia affairs is that those who are responsible for it do not seem to appreciate that fact, for they have permitted the militia force to remain in the same condition, and they are still receiving the mere pittance of fifty cents a. day that they did eight or ten years ago. I am sure the minister cannot escape responsibility for that action. I should be very sorry indeed, when in a nonpolitical way the member for Haldimand discussed the militia question, if it should afterwards be discussed from a party standpoint. His speech was not delivered in a partisan spirit; it was delivered rather with the idea of presenting, as the hon. gentleman did present, a faithful and truthful picture of the condition of the active militia of this country at the present time. If that picture has not been overdrawn, if that picture is true to life, as we must believe it is, in view of the statements he has made, may I ask my hon. friend from Alberta. who is an independent supporter of the government, can he congratulate himself upon the condition of things which exists



at the present time in that important department of the government ? Can any member of this House congratulate himself upon the statement made by the hon. member for Haldimand, that the force is fast crumbling into disorganization and decay 7
Just one word. I said the country force, the rural militia.

I have always supposed, and I have no reason to change my opinion, that the country part of the force was as much to be relied upon, was just as stalwart as any other part of the force; that it was an important and integral part of the force, the most numerous part of the force ; and if that integral part of the force is in the condition the hon. gentleman states, surely we cannot be charged with taking party advantage of the fact if we draw the attention of the responsible minister to that condition of affairs, and suggest that he should do something to remedy it ? That, I think, has been the head and front of the offending of which hon. gentlemen on this side of the House have been guilty. And was it not germane to the discussion which has taken place that the hon. member for East Elgin should draw attention to the report of the major general commanding the force 7 He was sent out here, I believe, to endeavour to make the militia force more efficient than it was, and it appears from the statements made by the hon. member for Haldimand that he was not sent out here any too soon. The Major General says in his report that he has forwarded another document to the Minister of Militia, drawing his attention to the condition of the militia force and making suggestions as to its improvement. Have the opposition not also the right to complain that, in a matter of so much importance, both sides of the House have been kept in the dark 7
While I do not wish to encourage a military spirit, I think we would be a spiritless people if, in a country like Canada, we did not establish and maintain an efficient militia force that would enable us at all times and under all circumstances to maintain the integrity of this country. AVe are not living here on sufferance, notwithstanding what has been said by hon. gentlemen on the other side. We are here, and we are here to stay, and we are going to maintain the integrity of this country at all times and at all hazards. And when we are told that the militia force of this country is only the shadow of a skeleton, I think it is high time we paid more attention to the administration of militia affairs than we have been doing during the past three or four years. Sir, it is a most regrettable thing to hear the statement made in this House that if, unfortunately, the integrity of Canada should be attacked, if our territory should be assailed from Europe, or by a European force, we Mr. CLARKE.
would have to look to the United States for protection. I hope never to live to see the day when that situation will present itself, when Canadians will have to depend upon the good offices of their cousins in the United States for the protection of the soil of Canada. We value too highly our connection with the great empire of which we form a part, we appreciate the privileges of a connection with that empire too highly, we realize too deeply the value we derive from that connection, to have any sympathy with such a view ; and we believe that if Canadians are not able to defend their own territory they have only to make an appeal, and that appeal will be responded to by men of all classes and races who comprise the empire, which is world-wide, and which has the strength, the power, the ability and the willingness to assist Canadians when Canadians are unjustly or unfairly assailed.
May I be permitted to point out, without indulging in any attempt to make party capital, that in view of the condition of militia affairs in this country, we ought not to embark on a scheme of naval defence unless we first make our militia force efficient. I regret exceedingly that we have not had a larger representation of the members of the cabinet here to-night to listen to the remarks of the member for Haldimand. I sincerely hope that those remarks will not have fallen upon deaf ears, and that before this session closes the suggestions which he has made will be taken up and acted upon, and that a reasonable sum will be placed in the estimates to give effect partially or wholly, to the views enunciated by the hon. member for Haldimand. I am satisfied that if that is done that the hon. member for Alberta and every hon. member on the other side of the House will find that, true to its traditions, the Conservative party will be willing, in days to come, as it has been in days gone by. to treat in a non-partisan way all matters affecting the welfare of the militia of Canada and pertaining to the defence of this country. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that it is practically wasting a million and three-quarters of dollars annually, the sum now voted for the militia force, if we cannot obtain better results than those which have been presented to us to-night. It would be better to adopt the suggestion of the member for Haldimand, and spend another quarter of a million dollars, making the total expenditure two millions, if, as a result of that additional expenditure, the militia force could be brought up to that state of efficiency which the hon. gentleman says would be the case if the pay of the men serving in the rural battalions were increased.

I am glad that the hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. Thompson! has made this proposal to

raise the pay of the volunteer force in Canada. It has been a great annoyance to the counties throughout the province of Ontario for many years that no sooner have the county councils got together in the month of June than the captains of the volunteer companies come before them and ask for twenty-five cents a day for the volunteers from that county. These counties who give the twenty-five cents extra, have not only to pay for their own volunteers, but they have also to bear the burden of general taxation to pay the volunteers of other counties. It is for the defence of the Dominion of Canada, and the whole Dominion of Canada has a right to support that defence.
I believe fifty cents a day is not enough for our militiamen and that it should be doubled The county which produces no volunteers has a perfect right to pay the taxes in support of the volunteers belonging to a county that produces volunteers and gives them twenty-five cents extra. I know that there will be no attempt on this side of the House to try to make political capital out of this question and I am surprised that a so-called independent member, when such a thing was not mentioned on this side of the House, should try to make it appear that we are finding fault with the government when it was an lion, member on their own side of the House who found fault with them. I have nothing more to say except to express the hope that this House will be unanimous in declaring that our [DOT] volunteers shall receive fair pay and that it will see that instead of leaving it to the county that produces the volunteers to produce the twenty-five cents extra as well that the Dominion of Canada shall be taxed to pay the volunteers.

speechtext: I wish to know from the minister what improvements in lighthouses -he intends making on the Lower St. Lawrence this year, and which are included in this vote of $322,000 ? All these lighthouses and aids to navigation which I have mentioned between Montreal and Quebec and between Quebec and the sea, have been recommended by those connected with navigation. I am informed by the chief engineer that every consideration has been given to the representations made as to the structure of the lighthouses. As to the colour of the lighthouses and as to the sloping roofs, all these have been considered by the department with a view to giving entire satisfaction to the shippers, and experiments are now being made. It is not a satisfactory explanation to say that the recommendation of the shipping people have been considered and that some people in Halifax have approved of certain aids to navigation established there. As regards the old - Bayfield,' I may say that as far back as 1900 there was a question of putting, a new engine in the steamer. This is the report of Mr Evans, on the steamer, made in 1900 :
If the department decides to fix up the engine now in her, I would suggest that a new foundation be put in and all bad frames under it and in that vicinity renewed, also some new beams forward of the boiler.
But if you decide to put in a new and modern engine I then would suggest that all ceiling be renewed and every bad or old timber be taken out and new work connected to the work that was done in 1896 at Port Dalhousie,' this will also include deck and deck frame and bottom plank.	.	, .	. ... ,
As regards my own opinion I do not thina the steamer in her present condition is worth putting a new engine of the modern type in, and I agree with Mr. Stewart on this point, as I am aware that there are many pa.rts^ of her that were put in the boat when first built.
I am also of the opinion that if the engine now in her can be made right, that it will be all right to fix her as I have described on that basis, and her ground tackle and out-fit are in
good condition.
(Sgd.) WM. EVANS.
This report of Mr. Evans was made after a report from Mr. Stewart, which was as follows ;
The [DOT] Bayfield,' Southampton, July 15, 1900.
Sir,-In forwarding Mr. Nisbet's report upon the information he obtained from the dismantling of his engine last week I can state I saw the worn out bolt and the weakened flange.
It is a difficult thing to suggest the best remedy for the present unsatisfactory state of affairs.
The engine and wooden boat are thirty-eight years old : for the first twenty years of their

lives they had the hardest kind of work in towing. Since we purchased the vessel nothing has been spent upon the machinery except for repairs that became absolutely necessary.
The cylinder has been bored out several times to make it true, but that cannot be done again, as the limit has been more than reached.
The bed plate of the engine is badly broken through the main bearing and is not worth the costly repairs necessary.
Then the boat is so old, a new engine could be used in her only a couple of years when it would have to be sold second hand, for a small sum. no matter in how a good repair it might be.
The boat is not large enough to temporarily accommodate an engine of size suitable for a larger boat, even if our old boiler could supply the necessary steam.
The boiler is now eighteen years old and can carry only eighty pounds steam. Our smokestack will have to be renewed in another year.
The present engine is a very extravagant one, she uses a ton of hard coal to steam twenty to twenty-five miles at. eight and a-half miles per hour, when a modern engine will easily steam thirty to thirty-five miles on a ton of soft coal at eleven and a-half miles per hour.
If the present engine frame could stand the extra power I should recommend steeple compounding, with of course a new cylinder, but it would be dangerous as the connections are not fit. When this engine was built, fifty pounds of steam was a large amount and the frame was probably built, for that, but it has been worked for years with a pressure of eighty to one hundred. The boat is too old for a new engine, the boiler has about lived its life and the engine is not worth the extensive repairs, the engineer says are necessary.
Should r be caught in heavy weather it is difficult to say what may happen.
I am. sir.
Your obedient servant,
(Sgd.) H'M. J. STEWART.
In 1901 there was another report, as follows :-
The repairs now being made to the hull of the ' Bayfield ' are of such a nature that she will probably last as long as her boiler, say four or five years.
In the Interest of greater economy and efficiency I would therefore strongly recommend that the old engine (now on the dock at Owon Sound) be replaced by a modern compound of greater power. The old engine was built in 1863. when the act of engine building, for economy, was not as well understood as it is at present. It consumes 300 tons hard coal per season, 100 of which ($500) could be saved by a properly constructed modern engine When under weigh now, the single crank causes a great deal of vibration and it is impossible even to write on board so that a. lot of time is lost. Most of this trouble would be removed bv a compound engine. With increased power there is no reason the steamer should not travel faster than seven and a-half knots, her present speed.
Should the department desire to sell the boat she would bring a small price in her present state, as a private party would have to compound the engine in order to run on a paying basis. With proper machinery in the now, rebuilt hull she would he much more valuable.

I certify that this is a correct copy of the letter of John Harrison & Sons Co., and a correct copy of Wm. Stewart's recommendation.

The matter is exactly where it was last night. The facts of the case are these:	The department had on
hand, this valuable boat. Some strong party friends-these Harrison people of Owen Sound-made application for the boat. They knew what had been done b,v the hon. gentleman in the case of the ' Dolphin.' They knew that party friends were practically made a present of that boat, and tbey desired to be treated in like manner. As far as Mr. Stewart is concerned, while he certainly had experience in sailing the boat, he

had tiot a single idea as to what its real value was. He was not a ship carpenter or steamboat engineer, and I have no doubt that there is in the hon. gentleman's department, in his private drawers, correspondence from these gentlemen, and probably from prominent Liberals In the riding, and in all probability from the defeated candidate, strongly urging that the boat must be handed over to the Harrisons without any competition. I repeat that if the hon. minister had spent $5 in advertising in the Owen Sound, Midland and Collingwood newspapers the fact that this boat was for sale, the department would have got 55,000 more than it did. These people were simply made a present of it, and are now using it in the business of towing logs. If the hon. gentleman proposes to conduct his department in the way this affair is being managed, he will not receive the commendation of people who wish to see the public funds and property properly administered.

There is no correspondence whatever in the department from the late candidate in the riding of any sort. And the transaction was perfectly fair and above board. Mr. Stewart wanted to dispose of the boat, and the officials of the department recommended that it be sold. The boat had been bought in 1884 for $14,000. It was thirty-eight years old, and the certificates I have laid on the Table show clearly to any business man that it was not fit for the service. As regards its sale for $3,250, I concluded to sell her at that price to Harrison & Sons, who were recommended to me as people able to pay the amount, and because it was considered by those competent to advise that the department would do well to sell it at that price. The boat was not delivered until the amount was paid.

speechtext: The letter you have just read refers to correspondence or previous negotiations.

- Mr. THOMSON (Grey). It is all the more remarkable that this course is pursued in the case of this vessel, because, two or three years ago a discussion was "aised in this House over the sale of the ' Dolphin ' under somewhat similar circumstances. She was sold without tender, and it was said that she was practically given away. The question was raised at that time, and the government was condemned for the course they pursued. Yet th_>y have dis-Mr. BENNETT.

And about a year ago the department spent about $3,000 in repairs, fitting her up with the most expensive quartered oak wainscotting, in fact she was fitted up in a most palatial manner. Yet we find the hon. minister disposing of this vessel, without tender, for a sum just about enough to pay for the repairs of the year before. There is something wrong about this transaction. I have had letters from Owen Sound, and I must say that it is news to the people there that this valuable vessel has practically been given away.

What they feel most keenly is that this valuable vessel should have been practically given away in the very face of what had been said in this House in regard to the sale of tlm ' Dolphin.' I must say that the explanation given by the hon. minister is very unsatisfactory.

From the information I received from my officers I suppose that he did. It was a fortunate thing for the government that this matter was treated in this artful way-not to have the correspondence speak for itself, but to have the negotiations partly in the form of a conversation. Once again I tell the minister that, having spoken to men who know this vessel and the value of it, I feel sure that this country has lost, by this transaction of the minister, from $3,000 to $5,000. I can tell the hon. gentleman also that if he wishes to retain any reputation for himself in the disposition of any property belonging to the people, he will sell it here-

after in a public manner, and not in this clandestine way.
The MINISTER OF alARINE AND FISHERIES. The only answer I can give to the hon. gentleman (Mr. Bennett) is that I am ready to take lessons and learn by experience. But the fact that hon. gentlemen opposite are not ready to go before the Public Accounts Committee and sift this matter, is a proof that, after all, this discussion is for the purpose of making more pages in ' Hansard ' and nothing else.

The hon. minister speaks of a business department and a business government. Wbat an absurdity it is to take up the time of the House with such nonsense. [DOT] He tells us the government were trying for two years to sell this vessel. Is not this a fine statement to make to intelligent men. when the government did not post up a bill or put an advertisement in a paper, as they might have done for five dollars, to let everybody know that the vessel was for sale ? The department, it appears, have been stewing and fretting about selling this vessel, after having spent about $3,000 in fitting her up in fine oak wain-scotting. And to explain the low price obtained for the steamer, the hon. minister says the vessel was condemned. Now, I would ask you, Mr. Chairman (Mr. Macdonald, Huron)-you know how you criticised transactions of the government when you were on this side-would any business department spend so much money on a vessel that was useless ? Why, it is the height of folly-and I would like to speak of it in stronger terms, but I refrain in view of the mild way in which you, Mr. Chairman, used to speak about such things. Then the hon. minister wants to know why we do not take the matter before the Public Accounts Committee. Why, what good would that do ? The documents are not there. The transaction was arranged partly in whispers and conversations that are not on record. If we attempted to make an investigation, no doubt, we should be treated as we have been treated in the Public Accounts Committee before. When a witness is asked a question that would incriminate a minister, he is told that he need not answer the* question. Why do we not take it before the Public Accounts Committee ? We do not need to. It is before the public of Canada, and they will realize quite handily, the absurdity of the defence submitted by the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries to this committee to-night.

I would like to ask if Mr. Stewart, who recommended the sale of the ' Dolphin ' for $700, is the same agent who recommended the expenditure of this $3,000 for refitting the ' Bayfield ' in palatial style, and also the same gentleman who recommended the sale of the ' Bayfield' to Messrs. Harrison & Son for $3,250 ?
