speechtext: Who is the gentleman that recommended the sale for $3,200 ?
Mr. W. J. Stewart. He is the gentleman in charge of the hydrographic survey, and he had charge of the boat. He has been in the employ of the department since 1884, he began with the boat.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: He might be in the employ of the department for fifty years and not know much about the value of vessels. I was talking about his experience and his knowledge of the value of vessels.
Mr. Stewart's recommendation was agreed to by Sir Charles Hibbert Tupper.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Does Sir Charles Hibbert Tupper say that Mr. Stewart is an expert in the value of vessels ?
Mr. Stewart is one of the best engineers in the country.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I was not talking about his ability as an engineer, but about his experience and knowledge of the value of vessels. He might be the best engineer in the world and not be capable of putting a value upon vessels. I have examined engineers in court dozens of times, when an attempt has been made to ascertain their knowledge of the value of vessels, and they either said they bad no knowledge or the court has excluded their evidence because they were uot supposed to be capable of forming an opinion. What I inquired was whether, in addition to his eminent ability as an engineer, he has any practical knowledge of the value of steamers of this character-because that is the whole question. Did the government obtain sufficient data from a competent person as to the value of this vessel before disposing of her ?

That boat was bought in 1884 at a cost of $14,000, and surely an engineer who has been on board that boat year after year and season after season, without knowing the value of the boat, would not be tit to be employed in the department, even as an engineer on the hydrographic survey. He was surely intelligent enough to learn, in the space of twenty years, the value of the boat on which he was employed. Year after year he knew what repairs were necessary on that boat, and recommended them. I have laid before the House certificates, letters and correspondence of the chief engineer as regards that boat. It appears by Mr. Stewart's report that I have laid on the Table, that he made a report when it was necessary to spend $3,000 to replace an old engine with a new one, showing that he knew what he was talking about. I do not know that any other opinion has been advanced against his own. A boat that has been in use for twenty years and been frequently repaired, could not be worth many thousands of dollars at the end of twenty years. Hon. gentlemen can go on talking about it and trying to make campaign literature, but I do not believe many people will take much stock in it, especially when they cannot show that there has been anything crooked in the matter. Why do they not go to the Public Accounts Committee if they want to show that there were favours granted to any particular individual, that it was a preconcerted arrangement to dispose of this boat by private sale ? If they cannot prove any of these things, I do not think they will be able to make much political capital.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: The hon. gentleman does not appear to know the functions of the Public Accounts Committee, because it is perfectly evident from his oft-repeated statement, that he thinks we can investigate in the Public Accounts Committee the necessity of advertising the sale of government property before disposing of it by private sale.
I never said we could investigate it in the Public Accounts Committee.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: He has said two or three times this evening that if we had any investigation to make into the circumstances under which this steamer ' Bayfield ' was sold, we can go and make it before the Public Accounts Committee. He does not know the functions of that commitee, because he ought to know that its functions are confined to looking into the expenditure of the past year, and are strictly limited to that by his own friends. We do not require any other campaign literature than the statement made by the hon. gentleman himself, that, after spending $3,000 in repairs upon this boat, it was disposer. of at private sale, without calling for tenders, for the sum of $3,200. I think that statement will be sufficient to show the public in what way matters are going on in his department.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: In the correspondence that the hon. gentleman read, I did not hear him read anything from Mr. Stewart recommending these repairs. Has the minister Mr. Stewart's recommendation on that point ?
I have not, but I will be able to find it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: He has brought down the correspondence that suited his own convenience. We find that over $3,000 was spent, and we wish to know on whose recommendation it was spent.
On the recommendation of the engineer ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Would that be in writing 7

What I have here is a report of the chief engineer of the 3rd of April, 1001:
The next time I have to do work with the minister I will suggest that we talk over together the question of providing a new steamer for the hydrographic surveys for the next year. It appears to me that the 'Bayfield' cannot he used after this year, as Lake Huron will be finished, and she certainly is not fit to go on to Lake Superior.
(Sgd.) W. P. A.
Chief Engineer.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: It was after that, that $3,000 was spent.
We had to keep her afloat, because we wanted her for the service, and we could not uo otherwise than keep her in repair.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: The hou. gentleman says that he purchased this steamer in 1884 for $14,000. Now, vessels on the Georgian bay which have been in the service for a longer period, are still in good repair.
The boat was already an old boat when we bought her, she was already over twenty years old.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: But the rougher parts were all built over again, and altogether about $15,000 had been spent to keep her in repair. These government vessels are all kept in first class order, like the Canadian Pacific Railway steamers, deteriorating very little each year. The fact remains that the minister disposed of this vessel with about $1,700 worth of instruments, after $3,000 worth of repairs were put on the year previous with her engines, boilers and all the outfit, for the sum of $3,250, by private sale.	[DOT]

The hon. gentleman is under a wrong impression. There were no instruments whatever, the boat was stripped, with .lust the necessary furniture left for the crew and nothing else. All the other instruments were taken away and they are in use now on the new ' Bayfield.'
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Who was it that induced Harrison & Son to come down here in connection with the purchase of that steamer ?
I do not know.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: The hon. minister does not mean to say that there was not some inducement given theni to come down and purchase that boat ?
They must have known that it was for sale. Mr. Stewart had been instructed to find a purchaser and I suppose it was on account of that they came here.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: The other night I called the attention of the hon. minister to another matter. I asked him if he intended to make a present of the valuable water front to some party friends of his in the town of Midland named Pratt & Co. Has he decided that he is going to give that water frontage to these people ?
The matter is under consideration.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Has he seen any parties within the last three or four days about it?
I do not know the parties even by name and I have not seen them.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Has the hon. minister not been interviewed about that water front at Midland within the last three or four days ?
I have seen nobody about it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Is there anything in writing in the hon. minister's department in reference to a grant to the Midland Coal Company of a portion of the water frontage that was sold to the town of Midland and handed over by it and upon which those parties have built a dock ?
There may be, but I do not remember.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: May I ask the hou. minister to ask his deputy if there is ?
I am informed by my deputy that he does not know.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Has there been any communication with the hon. minister himself by these parties as to this water frontage at Midland being granted to them ?
Not to my knowledge.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Well all I can say is that this seems to be a most extraordinary thing. Here was a most valuable piece of water frontage in Midland. It was vested in the Crown. It had not been deeded to any person. The town of Midland made an arrangement with the government, or with the Department of Public Works, that they would purchase this water frontage and hand it over to the Dominion government for the Dominion of Canada and in return for handing it over, they having paid $10,000 for the property, they were to have a dock erected upon it. A valuable portion of the property that the town thought they were to have, has been built upon by private individuals. They have built a most extensive dock upon it and the Department of Public Works has been dredging around it. Yet the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries tells the committee now that these parties have gone to work and constructed this $20,000 dock on Dominion government property and that they have not asked him anything about it. Is that a fact ?
It is a fact. I know nothing whatever about it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
Well, that seems to be a most extraordinary proceeding. Here is a piece of water front which was not vested in these parties. They had no more title

to it than I had, and I had no title to it whatever, and yet they have gone on and built this dock and X am told by men who are familiar with the transaction in the town that they have the assurance of the department that they are to have the property. Does the hon. minister ask me to believe that these people would think of building a dock upon this property without consulting his department as to whether they could have it or not ? It is nothing short of a scandal In that town and it will be a bigger scandal when I tell the people that the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries says that there has been no representation made to him about it, and that the parties have gone on and built that dock without consulting his department. If they have not consulted the hon. minister I say it is high time that the hon. minister put a notice on that property warning people that they should not trespass upon it by building docks upon it. Does the hon. minister propose to allow these parties to have it for nothing ?

I think my hon. friend (Mr. Bennett) must be altogether mistaken in the statements he has made in regard to the property transferred to the Crown by the municipality of Midland. I think probably my hon. friend the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Hon. Mr. Pr6-fortaine) Is not responsible for anything that was done in regard to it. The transaction commenced some considerable time ago- probably a year or more ago. There was a long negotiation. The council had to pass a by-law to acquire some property which they were to transfer to the Crown op certain conditions.
speakername: The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS (Hon. James Sutherland).

speechtext: I do not say that these parties have built a dock on all of the property that the Dominion government has had handed over to it by the town, but, there was a large wedge-shaped piece that the town had the assurance they were to have, and which was to become part of the property on which a public dock was to be built. On this portion which was never deeded by the Crown to any private individual, this dock has in part been built.

I do not agree with the hon. gentleman. When the papers are brought down I think they would show that my recollection of the matter is correct. A very considerable time elapsed before the by-law was voted upon and carried and the town was prepared to pay the owners of the property that was to be transferred. I think the hon. gentleman's firm were acting as solicitors for the corporation. There was a considerable correspondence with the Department of Marine and Fisheries, or perhaps the Department of Justice, in regard to the title and the description of the property. I feel safe in saying, that no pro-
perty which was deeded to the Crown has been taken with the authority of the department by private individuals. It seems impossible that such a thing could have taken place.

The hon. Minister of Public Works misunderstands my point. There was a wedge-shaped portion, a very valuable piece of water frontage which was under the Crown, and which had never been deeded to any private party. Two different parties were contending for it. One of the parties who made a claim for it was the party who was selling to the town and when the town was buying from this private party it was -well understood that the department would not deed that to the other party. Instead of it being reserved for the Crown some political friends of hon. gentlemen opposite have erected a dock upon it. May I ask the hon. Minister of Public Works, as the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries knows nothing about it, if it has been arranged that any part of the water frontage which had not been deeded to any person is to be handed over to this coal company ?

My recollection of the matter which came before the department a year or so ago was that there was a dispute as to who had the title from the provincial government, when the provincial government were supposed to have the right to give a title to these water fronts, and it was claimed by the clients of the hon. gentleman and also by another party. I remember the matter was under consideration when I went to the department, and after very carefully hearing all parties and their solicitors, I think I came to the conclusion that it was right that the grant should be made to the parties who had purchased that portion of the water front from the original owners who had received the grant from the provincial government. At the time, it was contested by the parties and their solicitors, but I have never heard that that was not a fair decision in the interest of all parties concerned. I am not sure whether that grant was consummated to the parties that we decided were entitled to it as a matter of justice and right. I am perfectly satisfied that when the property was transferred to the Crown by the town of Midland, no part of that property has been transferred to any person. The hon. gentleman will remember that we had a good deal of trouble about the description and that engineers were sent there and the description amended. I believe that everything was done to protect the interest of the Crown and to do what was right by the parties. It does not follow that because the minister and the officers of the department decided on the claim of one party as against the claim of another, that any injustice was done. It would have to be clearly shown

that a mistake had been made before they could have been accused of such a thing. I am perfectly satisfied that when the plans and titles are examined, it will be found that no part of the property transferred to the Crown by the town of Midland has been interfered with or is occupied by any person else. If so, it is without authority. As this is under the joint jurisdiction of the Marine Department and the Department of Public Works I was particularly careful to have a report from the chief engineer before permission was given to the people who owned the water lots to build, in order that it should not interfere with navigation and the prospect of improvement there, which I believe will be great. I personally felt that it was desirable in the public interest that we should be careful in giving permission for the erection of docks, and any action that was taken was taken after careful investigation and report by the chief engineer. I do not think that any mistake has been made. Everything that was done was done by the officers of the department in what they understood to be the public interest. There was no political influence or favouritism about it. Nor do I know that the minister or the officers knew particularly who were interested in these works. The parties were represented by solicitors and we had a great contest over the ownership. I feel satisfied that the papers will show that the public interest has been carefully protected and that no favouritism has been shown to one party or the other. I think my hon. friend will admit that so far as political friends or clients are concerned, I showed no partisanship in the matter and that there was no public favouritism in it. It was desirable that we should undertake very substantial improvements at once which in the near future we hope to very greatly extend. If any mistake has been made, it was not because of political feeling, because everything was done under the advice of the officers of the department, after careful investigation.

The minister is mistaken in saying that I was acting professionally for either of the parties. When I saw the minister I represented the town, because it was particularly asked by the town that in view of the fact that they were giving this large sum of 810,000 for the water frontage they should have this wedge-shaped piece as well. The town was buying the adjoining piece for $10,000, to hand over to the government, and the wedgeshaped piece was to be reserved by the Crown. It now turns out that it has been granted to these gentlemen without any consideration, and it goes without saying that they are strong political friends of the government. Had the people of the town understood that they were not to have the property that this dock had been built upon, the by-law for $10,000 would never have been
carried. It was clearly understood that the town was to have it in addition to the property they were buying from Burton Bros., who were represented, I think, by the hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. McCarthy)- because when the minister showed me the file, the correspondence was between the member for North Simcoe and the department. I was not acting for either party. On the one hand Burton Bros, were claiming the wedge-shaped piece ; and a gentleman named Jeffrey was claiming it also, and the town was asking that as they were buying the Burton property, for the large sum of $10,000, and as the wedge-shaped piece was in the Crown, that the Crown should not give it to any person, but should let it go with the other property. It now turns out, to the surprise of every one in Midland, that instead of the government reserving this wedge-shaped piece, and adding that to the property handed over to the Crown, the Crown have given it to another party. That action is going to interfere very materially with the prospect of the dock being of general utility to the public.
The hon. gentleman has referred to the application made in the name of Mrs. Jeffery.
I referred to her husband.

I did not know that Mr. Jeffery was in the matter. I remember distinctly that the previous owners to whom the Burton Bros, were heirs had sold the water lot, described by metes and bounds. The statement they made to me was that they had not sold it to the deep water, but they wanted the Crown to transfer to them the front of the lot on which the people had built the dock, so that practically they could not use the dock. It seemed to me a most unfair and unjust proposition. When they sold the water lot it was fully intended that it should go to deep water, and the parties had no right in law or justice to anything between the dock that the people had built on the lot they bought and paid for, and deep water. They had sold that piece of property upon which these people had expended their money, and then they wanted to deprive them of the use of it. The dock would be no use if you were to take the water, and that water did not belong to them anyway, but to the Crown. In my opinion they had no right to it at all, and it would be an injustice to deprive the others of it. As to the effect upon the harbour from the public standpoint, there is a difference of opinion between my hon. friend (Mr. Bennett) and the officers of the department. I am not personally responsible for that, except in so far as I took the advice of the officers of the department after careful consideration. I believe that the permission given by the Department of Public Works

will not interfere with navigation or with the use of the harbour from a public point of view.

The minister has misunderstood me. What I say is that by reason of their encroaching upon this property, when the department builds their docks there they will be very much limited in space and it will be very detrimental to the harbour. However, we can discuss the matter on the Public Works estimates.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The minister is to get the papers which he promised in reference to Mr. Hurley's report.

I did not promise any papers.
I read the report of the Deputy Minister of Marine and Fisheries containing the verbal reports which he had taken from Mr. Hurley.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I want some information with reference to tjie duties of Mr. Hurley and the work he has done.
I have no other report than what was contained in the report of the deputy minister.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Then the hon. gentleman is paying a man $1,200 a year, and he has not a scratch of a pen to show what he has done for his money, what lakes he has visited or anything else. I want to know what waters Mr. Hurley has visited, and what work he has done. That report is simply a report made by the deputy minister ; there is nothing from Mr. Hurley in it.
The deputy minister has reported on the work done by Mr. Hurley. That is all I have.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I assume that the committee is still considering the item of $322,000 for the construction of lighthouses. Early in the session I took the liberty of calling the attention of the Minister of Public Works to a matter in my own county, not knowing at that time, in the somewhat disturbed condition of affairs, whether the construction of lighthouses would be under the Minister of Public Works or the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. I was directed by the Minister of Public Works to let the matter stand until the Minister of Marine and Fisheries brought down his estimates. What I referred to was an old standing promise made by some one in the year 1900 that a lighthouse would be erected on the new dock that was being built by the government at the port of Bronte, in the county of Halton. This was freely referred to during the election of 1900, and the people there were assured that one of the advantages of electing my opponent would be that they would secure a lighthouse at this point. What I wish to ask the minister now is to

.see that that assurance, on which the votes of the electors were obtained, shall be carried out. I need not tell the minister that a lighthouse at that point would be a very desirable thing-not so much perhaps for the purpose of guiding vessels passing in and out of the port, because there is not a great deal of traffic, particularly in the night, in that part of Lake Ontario. But this port is a fishing station, and the Minister of Marine and Fisheries is interested in fisheries as well as in marine matters. The town of Bronte is the chief seat of the cisco herring fisheries. There are a considerable number of fishermen living there, who have a considerable quantity of plant, vessels and nets, and they have occasion to go out for a distance of ten or fifteen miles to set their nets and obtain their catch. These people are frequently caught out at night at some distance, espeeialy in the autumn, in stormy weather in the open lake, with nothing to guide them back to port. For the purpose of indicating to these men where to return to, a lighthouse would certainly be a very desirable thing, and I feel very much like the gentleman who promised that a lighthouse would be erected there, in pressing it upon the attention of the government although possibly not for the same reason that he may have ha^l. I do not know whether the attention of the minister has been drawn to this matter by the gentleman who exercises the patronage of that county. I do not claim to exercise it. It is possible that he has not been allowed to forget the-promise he made at that time ; but I regret very much to have noticed, when the hon. minister read the items of expenditure throughout the province of Ontario for the erection of lighthouses, that the important port of Bronte was overlooked entirely. I do not know whether it will appear in the supplementary estimates or not : but as it does not appear in the main estimates, I trust that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries will not forget this important port, and will place in the supplementary estimates a sufficient sum to construct a lighthouse at this point. I am quite sure that if he knew all the circumstances, his generosity, his good nature and his desire to meet the views of his political friends, if nothing else, would induce him to do something for the relief of those people, who will appreciate any kindness in that direction which he can accord to them. I hope and trust, if the minister's attention has not been drawn to it before, that now that I have mentioned it, possibly for the third time, he will take a note of it. and that before another session passes over the people of Bronte will be delighted to have something which will guide them in the open lake in the dark nights to their homes.
Will the hon. gentleman tell me who made the promise and when it was made ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I do not like to mention the name of the gentleman who made the promise, but common rumour said it was made by the candidate who opposed me at the last general election. Whether he made it on his own responsibility or on the assurance of the government, I am not able to say, but I think that the hon. minister has sufficient ingenuity to divine, just as well as X can, the reason why the promise was made. Perhaps it was because I was elected that the lighthouse was not built, but it seems to me that when a promise is made to the electors it should be carried out. The people of Bronte, believing, no doubt, that this promise would be implemented by the government, gave a very strong support to my opponent, and on that ground are fully entitled to consideration even though their candidate was not elected. Hon. members know who my opponent was and the circumstances under which the promise was given. It is one of those promises that should be implemented by the governmnt and these people should not be disappointed.

The chief engineer of the department tells me that there is no correspondence whatever with regard to the establishment of a light at Bronte. If a demand be made, it will be examined on its merits by the engineer and a rexiort duly made. If the light be required-and the hon. gentleman has made out a very good case in favour of these poor fishermen-no doubt the department will furnish it, but at present no action can be taken because there is no record of any demand being made for a light at that place.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I trust the hon. minister will pardon me if I very humbly and meekly made the demand.
The bon. gentleman had better make it in writing.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I shall be very happy to do so if the hon. minister will give me any assurance that my request will receive the consideration of the government. No doubt the hou. gentleman has heard what I have said, and even though I should not communicate with him directly, his officers will learn from * Hansard ' the representations I have made, but I am quite willing to remind the hon. gentleman of what I have said and what the people would like very much to have, and I can assure him that they would be very grateful to the new minister if he should see fit to grant their request.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Has the hon. minister the papers with regard to Mr. Mullens ?
I beg to lay on the Table the tenders and articles of agreement between the department and Mr. Cornelius Mullens, of Belleville. One is dated 1st July, 1902, and the other 25th April, 1899.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: These two maps which the hon. minister has laid on the Table are very confusing. In view of the importance of the question of improvement which we are discussing, we are entitled to have something which would show us the present state of improvements on the St. Lawrence route. Evidently this map was prepared before June, 1902.
Whatever is marked ill black has been done and wliat is marked in red is to be done. It was brought up to date.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
I think I heard the hon.
gentleman refer to the lightship at Anticosti, has that been terminated ?
The	MINISTER	OF	MARINE	AND
FISHERIES. No, it will be on the 1st of September.

Have the steel rails been erected which are contemplated at Isle aux Raisins.
The	MINISTER	OF	MARINE	AND

There is a gas buoy in the centre of Lake St. Peter.
The	MINISTER	OF	MARINE	ANDFISHERIES. That	is	placed. It	was
on the 13th of this month.

Are the gas buoys between Longueuil and Contrecoeur jilaced ?
The	MINISTER	OF	MARINE	AND
FISHERIES. Some have not been delivered, but they have all been ordered. They are bought from the Pintscli Company, in Montreal.
Something was said last year .about experimenting with acetylene gas. What has been the result ?
Some of the acetylene lights have been successful and others have not. What we are using is mostly the Pintscli gas.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

There are six acetylene gas lights in the lighthouses.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
Wliat did it cost to iustal this carbide apparatus in a lighthouse ?
The	MINISTER	OF	MARINE	AND

Mr.	MONK. Are they purchased by
tender ?

Are they all purchased from the same person ?
The	MINISTER	OF	MARINE	AND

Taking this section between Montreal and Quebec, what is the amount the hon. gentleman expected to spend upon gas buoys and what upon lighthouses during the coming season ? I see there is exactly the same estimate as last year.
Twenty thousand dollars on each.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: And in the section below Quebec-Quebec to the gulf ?
About $180,000, including $95,000 for the light-ship at Anticosti.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: What remains now to be carried out of the suggestions made by the shipping interests ?
All that is in red on the map shown to the hon. gentleman (Mr. Monk).
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Perhaps it would be better if the hon. minister would mention in a general way what they are.
I read the list.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
The hon. gentleman read a list of what he intended to do. I asked what remains to be done to carry out the suggestion of the shipping interests, which he has told us he intended to carry out.
The SIINISTER OF S1ARINE AND FISHERIES. This will carry out practically all the suggestions of the shipping interests. I must say that that will not be all the improvements contemplated. For instance, the lighting between Sorel and Quebec cannot be completed, as it will be completed during the present season between Sorel and Montreal, until the channel is widened and so improved that it can be navigated at night without danger. We Hon. Mr. PREFONTAINE.
expect to have the lighting of the channel between Sorel and Montreal, forty-five miles, completed by the first of August. Vessels will then be able to navigate that part of the channel safely, day or night.

Is that with the improvements mentioned in this map ?
The	MINISTER	OF	MARINE	AND
FISHERIES. Yes.

Then, with the improvements mentioned in this map, there will be night navigation between Montreal and Sorel '!	.
The	MINISTER	OF	MARINE	AND
FISHERIES. There will be safe navigation day and night between Montreal and Sorel.

I think the hon. minister will see Alie advantage in future, in bringing down an estimate of this importance, of giving to us in a little clearer way on the maps, if he chooses to place maps on the Table, exactly what improvements are intended.
The	MINISTER	OF	MARINE	AND
FISHERIES. If the hon. member (Mr. Monk) would suggest in what way it could he made clearer. I should be glad to carry out his ideas. I am here to learn.

According to the map. all the gas buoys between Montreal and Sorel are to be established. But the hon. gentleman tells us that half of them have been established. I do not wish to take up the time of the committee in this way. Of course, I might put the hon. minister upon examination, and he will turn to his assistant for information and then will tell me that these are being carried out. The map does not show what is completed and what is contemplated.

If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Monk) leaves my estimates pending for three months, with the work going on during that time, I can hardly keep the information up to date in the form he wishes. I cannot make a new map every day. I have stated that one of these lights was installed as lately as the 18th of this month. If the channel is to be completely lighted between Montreal and Sorel before the 1st of August, the hon. gentleman must suppose that the work is going on.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I see from the map that at Cape Race a syren and quick flashing light have been recommended. Has that been carried out ?
It will be done this year but has not been completed yet.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

That is a matter to be considered with the imperial government.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I do not wish to take up my hon. friend's (Hon. Mr. Prdfontaine) time in this matter. I can only say that I do not think he has taken as great an interest in transportation as he pretends to have done.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The hon. minister has brought down the papers in reference to Mr. Mullens, and I must say that they go to corroborate the statement of my hon. friend from Grenville (Mr. Reid). In 1899, the former Minister of Marine and Fisheries Sir Louis Davies, called for tenders for this work for three years. The tenders came iu and that of Mr. Mullens was accepted. His contract expired in March, 1902, and without a word, so far as the correspondence shows, that contract was renewed for three years. This was evidence on the face of it that the contract was renewed for a consideration. And that consideration was what my hon. friend from Hastings (Mr. Porter) says-that Mr. Hurley was to secure that contractor a renewal of his contract if he would sign the protest. If that were not the case, no doubt there would Ije correspondence to show it.

I am informed by the officers of the department that it has been the invariable practice to renew a contract of this kind if the work was properly performed. That course was pursued in this case, and Mr. Hurley had nothing whatever to do with it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Has there been any reduction in insurance rates on the St. Lawrence route during last year ?

I am informed that the new Canadian Pacific Railway fleet have been granted better rates than those charged in former years. The reason given was that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, having acquired the Elder-Dempster and some other boats, were offering more guarantee, it was said, than other companies before them, and also that the insurers believed the representations made to them that the channel was very much improved, and these reductions could be safely made.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: When a lighthouse is constructed, is the contract given for the house only ? Is the lighting part installed by the department itself ?

If it is a lighthouse in the water; when a pier has to be constructed, we make a contract for the construction of a pier, or, sometimes, if we think it cheaper, having our own men, we build the pier ourselves. If the superstructure is in wood, 181
it is given by contract. If there are a number to be built and the superstructure is iron or steel, a general contract is 'given for these, tenders being asked for. The lanterns are bought by the department from the best makers in England, and are bought at the market prices which are published in the newspapers.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: What explanation would the minister give of the term ' guaranteed ' there ? What guarantee were they offered ?
Proper equipment, I suppose, and better boats, better captains.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: When this item was up for consideration last year the minister stated that the large increase in the expenditure for lighting the St. Lawrence would result iu a reduction of the insurance rates. Has the minister any information that because of that large expenditure on the lighting system of the St. Lawrence route, reductions have; been made in insurance rates during the past year ? I may say that it is not possible that those would apply only to the Canadian Pacific Railway steamers.

I reason on this matter as any business man would from the facts. The facts are that the shipping interests for many years have been complaining that the St. Lawrence route was not safe, and that they were charged too high insurance rates. They approached the government four or five years ago, and represented that they could get no reduction in rates unless there were improvements in the lighting and buoying of the St. Lawrence. The government undertook to make improvements, which have been going on since then, and now we find that the navigation companies are satisfied, that the shipping interests are satisfied. We know that the government have made' great efforts to improve the St. Lawrence-route and to put it in proper shape. All these facts of course are reported to the insurance companies daily, and we are justified in concluding that the rates will diminish. The; underwriters will no longer be able to urge that the channel is in a bad condition, that the lighting is insufficient. All these facts tend to convince the underwriters that they should reduce tlieir rates.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: The fact is that there has been no reduction in insurance rates up to the present moment.

It has been reported, I do not know it officially, that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company had obtained better rates than other companies. Now the fact that the shipping companies are not complaining, but on the contrary are expressing their satisfaction about the channel, would seem to indicate that these rates are reduced.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
To return a moment to the repairs on the steamer ' Bay-held ' I was surprised to hear the minister state that the repairs were much less than stated in the Auditor General's Report. I had not the Auditor General's Report before me at the moment, and was unable to put the figures before the House. In the meantime I have procured the Auditor General's Report for 1901. I can inform the hon. gentleman that in 1901 over $3,300 were expended for repairs on the * Bayfield,' and thati sum does not include the salary paid to the carpenter, which was over $300. In 1902, there were spent over $1,300 on the 'Bayfield.' In 1902, the carpenter was paid $472. So that altogether, in 1901 and 1902. $4,633 were expended in repairs on this boat. If you add the carpenters salary we have a total of $5,405. I find in the amount a compass bought in Glasgow for $219. I would like to know if the compass went with the vessel.
Some resolutions reported.

Would the hon. Minister of Finance give us the order of business for the day after to-morrow ?
The right hon. Prime Minister, in answer to a question yesterday, I think, stated that the business would be the Railway Bill.
All day ?
Well, perhaps in a short time we will get through it.
